questions.subTitle: Ergonomics
questions.text: A warning label is redesigned so that it carries its message through a symbol as well as a colour, so users with colour vision deficiency still receive it. Which of the five ergonomic qualities does this most directly improve?

options.A: Efficient
options.B: Usable
options.C: Effective
options.D: Safe

questions.commentary: Effective means the user achieves an accurate and complete result. Repeating the message through a second channel ensures the information actually reaches every user rather than only those who can distinguish the colour. Efficient refers to the effort or time a task costs, usable to whether the target population can operate the product at all, and safe to the risk of injury during use.

questions.subTitle: Anthropometrics
questions.text: A designer measures how far a seated operator can sweep an arm sideways before the shoulder lifts. This measurement is:

options.A: Static (structural) anthropometric data
options.B: Dynamic (functional) anthropometric data
options.C: Psychological data
options.D: Physiological threshold data

questions.commentary: Dynamic (functional) anthropometrics are taken while the body moves, and they capture reach envelopes, range of motion and step length. Static (structural) data such as seated eye height or shoulder breadth is taken with the body still. Dynamic data is harder to collect but usually more useful when designing controls, handles and workspaces.

questions.subTitle: Anthropometrics
questions.text: Which statement best explains why there is no "average human"?

options.A: Anthropometric data only applies to children
options.B: Standard deviation is always zero
options.C: Percentiles only work for height, not weight
options.D: Body dimensions do not always stay in the same proportion; a tall person can have short arms

questions.commentary: Body dimensions vary independently of each other. A person who is 50th percentile for height may be 80th percentile for shoulder width and 30th percentile for arm length. No single individual is average across every dimension at once, so a product sized for a fictional "average" person fits very few real people well.

questions.subTitle: Percentiles
questions.text: A vehicle restraint system is developed and validated using crash data from a 50th percentile male only. What is the main design risk?

options.A: Injury patterns are the same across the population, so no risk arises
options.B: Occupants whose proportions and mass differ from that single reference, such as smaller adults, are protected less effectively
options.C: The restraint will be over-engineered for every occupant
options.D: The data will be valid only for occupants above the 95th percentile

questions.commentary: Designing around one mid-range figure tunes the product to a user who represents nobody but themselves. Restraint geometry, belt loading and airbag timing all depend on stature, seated height and mass, so an occupant well away from the reference figure sits outside the conditions the system was validated for. This is why safety-critical dimensions are set against a percentile range, and why the range has to be drawn from the population that will actually use the product.

questions.subTitle: Percentiles
questions.text: A public library fits a fixed-height standing counter for its catalogue terminals. The counter cannot be adjusted, and users stand at it briefly. Which percentile should its working height be set to?

options.A: 5th percentile, so that the shortest users can reach the surface
options.B: 50th percentile, because the dimension cannot be adjusted and either extreme would penalise everyone at the other end
options.C: 95th percentile, so that the tallest users are not forced to stoop
options.D: 99th percentile, so that the whole population is covered

questions.commentary: Clearances are set to the largest user and reaches to the smallest, but a fixed working height is neither. It is a dimension where being too high and being too low are both uncomfortable, so the error is shared rather than pushed onto one end of the population. Setting the counter at 95th percentile height leaves shorter users working at shoulder level; setting it at 5th forces taller users to stoop. The 50th percentile keeps the worst mismatch as small as possible. It fits nobody exactly, which is why an adjustable surface is preferred wherever the cost can be justified.

questions.subTitle: Adjustability
questions.text: Which statement best explains why a designer would choose a range of sizes rather than adjustability?

options.A: A range of sizes accommodates 100% of the population
options.B: Adjustable products cannot accommodate 95th percentile users
options.C: The product is worn rather than shared, so adjusting mechanism would be impractical or too costly
options.D: Adjustability can only ever be applied to seating

questions.commentary: A range of sizes suits products that are worn or consumed rather than shared between users, and products where a mechanism would add unjustified cost or complexity. Helmets and clothing are the standard examples. Adjustability is preferred where one product must fit several different users in turn, such as an office chair or a car seat. Neither strategy reaches 100% coverage.

questions.subTitle: Work Envelopes
questions.text: A designer is setting the knee clearance under a desk and the distance from the seated user to an emergency stop button. Which percentiles are appropriate?

options.A: 95th for the knee clearance, 5th for the stop button distance
options.B: 5th for the knee clearance, 95th for the stop button distance
options.C: 50th for both
options.D: 95th for both

questions.commentary: Clearance is a 95th percentile problem: if the largest user fits under the desk, everyone does. Reach is a 5th percentile problem: if the user with the shortest reach can hit the stop button, everyone can. A single percentile cannot solve both at once, which is one reason adjustable workstations exist.

questions.subTitle: Physiology
questions.text: A rubber jar opener with a serrated metal strip helps users by:

options.A: Increasing the jar's weight
options.B: Reducing the lid diameter
options.C: Changing the colour of the lid
options.D: Increasing friction and providing mechanical advantage

questions.commentary: The rubber increases friction between hand and lid, so less squeezing force is wasted on slipping. The tool also acts as a lever, since a larger radius produces greater torque for the same hand force. Together these let users with reduced grip strength open jars with far less effort, reducing fatigue and injury risk.

questions.subTitle: Physiology
questions.text: An ergonomic keyboard with a wrist support and a split key arrangement is designed to reduce:

options.A: Eye strain
options.B: Muscle fatigue in the lower back during long periods of seated work
options.C: Strain on the wrists and hands during prolonged use
options.D: Colour confusion

questions.commentary: The split layout reduces the outward bending of the wrist that a straight keyboard forces, and the wrist rest reduces pressure on the carpal tunnel. Both address a physiological problem: repetitive strain caused by sustained awkward posture during extended use.

questions.subTitle: Psychology
questions.text: A phone gives a short vibration when a touchscreen button is pressed. The main ergonomic purpose of this vibration is to:

options.A: Reduce the force needed to operate the button
options.B: Confirm the input registered without relying on sight or sound
options.C: Increase the visual contrast of the button
options.D: Make the device audible in a noisy environment

questions.commentary: A touchscreen gives no mechanical travel, so without haptic feedback the user has no physical signal that the press registered, which leads to repeated presses and missed inputs. Haptics supply that confirmation through touch, which is why they work in silent mode and for users who are not looking at the screen. Their limit is that the sensation is weakened if the device rests on a surface rather than in the hand.

questions.subTitle: Psychology
questions.text: An Xbox controller contains small motors that vibrate in response to events on screen, such as an impact or the rumble of an engine. This is an example of:

options.A: Texture
options.B: Haptic feedback
options.C: Biomechanics
options.D: Anthropometrics

questions.commentary: The controller is delivering information through the sense of touch, timed to what the player is doing and seeing, which is what makes it feedback rather than decoration. Texture is a fixed property of a surface that the user feels passively, whatever the game is doing. Biomechanics concerns the forces and movements of the body itself, and anthropometrics is the measurement of body dimensions. Both matter to how the controller is shaped, but neither describes a signal sent back to the user.

questions.subTitle: UCD Foundation
questions.text: A project can begin either from a user problem the team has observed or from a new technology the team wants to find a use for. Which is the more reliable route to a successful product?

options.A: The observed user problem, because a product that resolves a difficulty people already have is adopted more readily
options.B: The new technology, because the most technically advanced product wins the market
options.C: Neither, because regulation determines which products succeed
options.D: Neither, because adoption cannot be anticipated at the design stage

questions.commentary: The two routes are usually called market pull and technology push. Need-driven development starts with evidence that a problem exists and is worth solving, so the product has a user before it has a specification. Technology-push products can succeed, but they carry the extra risk of having to create the demand as well as the solution, which is the basic argument for researching users before generating concepts.

questions.subTitle: UCD Foundation
questions.text: Research shows that the operators of a machine will always be wearing thick protective gloves. In UCD terms, this finding is best classified as a:

options.A: Want
options.B: Need
options.C: Limitation
options.D: Population stereotype

questions.commentary: Limitations are the physical, mental, cultural and technological constraints that define what is possible for this user in this situation. Gloves restrict dexterity and increase finger size, so they constrain control size and spacing. A need is what the user must be able to do, and a want is a preference that can be traded off.

questions.subTitle: UCD Process
questions.text: In the UCD process, which stage involves formal user testing with a broader range of end users, often guided by psychologists?

options.A: Research
options.B: Concept
options.C: Design
options.D: Implementation

questions.commentary: Implementation is where the product is built or manufactured and formal testing runs with a wider range of end users than the smaller studies of the earlier stages. Findings feed back into the design and into the instruction manual. Launch continues the process through customer feedback and post-launch questionnaires.

questions.subTitle: UCD Process
questions.text: Which of the following is a disadvantage of user-centred design?

options.A: It increases the number of late-stage redesigns
options.B: Relying heavily on user feedback tends to produce incremental improvement rather than breakthrough
options.C: It prevents designers from considering accessibility
options.D: It removes the need for prototyping

questions.commentary: Users can only respond to what they already know, so feedback tends to refine an existing product rather than suggest a new one. The other genuine disadvantages are the cost and time of research at every stage, conflicting findings that have to be judged rather than obeyed, and the difficulty of coordinating several disciplines. Reducing late redesigns is an advantage of UCD, not a disadvantage.

questions.subTitle: Multidisciplinary Teams
questions.text: A team developing a pressurised life-support garment is made up of engineers, a physician, a biologist and a materials specialist rather than engineers alone. The main advantage of this composition is that:

options.A: A single discipline reaches a solution faster without outside input
options.B: Material choice alone decides whether the garment succeeds
options.C: The strongest concept often comes from a discipline outside the obvious one, and the disciplines combine into solutions none would reach alone
options.D: Technical development can be led by marketing

questions.commentary: A multidisciplinary team builds understanding of the user, the task and the environment from several directions at once, which is why the decisive idea frequently arrives from an unexpected discipline. In the Mercury spacesuit programme the most effective concept came from a biologist rather than an engineer, and the thermal shell, closed-loop life support and biomed access all depended on combining fields. The cost is that more perspectives take longer to manage and usually mean more iterations.

questions.subTitle: Research Methods
questions.text: Which research method observes users in their authentic environment in order to capture cultural influences and habitual behaviour?

options.A: Survey
options.B: Focus group
options.C: Structured interview
options.D: Field research

questions.commentary: Field research takes the researcher into the home, workplace or shop where the product is actually used, revealing habits so automatic that users would never think to report them. Its main limitation is that the presence of an observer can change the behaviour being studied.

questions.subTitle: Research Methods
questions.text: A team breaks the operation of a ticket machine into a hierarchy of smaller steps in order to locate the point at which users hesitate or make errors. This method is:

options.A: Task analysis
options.B: Field research
options.C: A focus group
options.D: A Likert survey

questions.commentary: Task analysis breaks a complex task into a hierarchy of sub-tasks to show where friction occurs and how much the user has to hold in mind at each stage. It maps the structure of the task, which is also its limitation: it says nothing about the user's attitudes or motivations.

questions.subTitle: Research Methods
questions.text: A focus group differs from a survey mainly because a focus group:

options.A: Generates quantitative data that can be averaged
options.B: Can be distributed to thousands of participants
options.C: Uses moderated discussion to gather in-depth qualitative data
options.D: Does not require a moderator

questions.commentary: A focus group is a moderated discussion with roughly 6 to 10 selected participants, and the interaction between them surfaces views that individual responses would miss. A survey reaches far more people and produces numbers, but it cannot ask a follow-up question. The risk in a focus group is that one dominant participant skews the discussion.

questions.subTitle: Personas & Stereotypes
questions.text: Which of the following best describes a persona in UCD?

options.A: A real user recruited to test the final product
options.B: A fictional but research-based profile representing a target user group
options.C: A photograph of an average customer
options.D: A profile based on the designer's personal experience of the product

questions.commentary: A persona is a composite built from patterns that appeared across many real users, given a name, age, occupation, goals and frustrations so the team has a specific person to design for. It is neither a real individual nor the designer's own assumptions. Its weaknesses are that it dates quickly and that a poorly researched persona carries stereotypes straight into the design.

questions.subTitle: Personas & Stereotypes
questions.text: In the UK a light switch is pushed down for on, while in the USA it is pushed up. This difference is an example of:

options.A: A population stereotype
options.B: A design error
options.C: A universal standard
options.D: A failed usability test

questions.commentary: Population stereotypes are learned expectations about how controls should behave, produced by standardisation within a society rather than by anything intrinsic to the device, so neither convention is objectively correct. They matter most in safety-critical design, because under stress users fall back on the deeper habit rather than the convention they recently learned.

questions.subTitle: Fidelity
questions.text: Why do designers usually test with low-fidelity prototypes before building anything at high fidelity?

options.A: Low-fidelity models give more accurate data on structural performance
options.B: Changes are still cheap at that stage, and a rough model invites criticism rather than approval
options.C: Low-fidelity models are required for regulatory approval
options.D: High-fidelity prototypes cannot be shown to users

questions.commentary: Low-fidelity prototypes are quick, cheap and easy to discard, so an idea can be rejected before anyone has invested in it. A high-fidelity model looks finished, which discourages the criticism the test was meant to collect, and by then modifications cost almost as much as a redesign. High fidelity is reserved for final user testing, stakeholder presentations and approval.

questions.subTitle: Drawings
questions.text: In third-angle orthographic projection, where is the top view placed relative to the front view?

options.A: Above the front view
options.B: Below the front view
options.C: To the left of the front view
options.D: To the right of the front view

questions.commentary: Third-angle projection, used in the USA, Canada and Australia, places each view on the side of the front view that it represents, so the top view sits above and the right-side view sits to the right. First-angle projection, used in the UK and Europe, arranges the views the opposite way round.

questions.subTitle: Physical vs Virtual
questions.text: A team needs to judge whether a handheld tool balances correctly in the hand. Which approach is more appropriate, and why?

options.A: A virtual prototype, because it can be iterated far more quickly
options.B: A virtual prototype, because it can simulate extreme loading conditions
options.C: A physical prototype, because weight and balance cannot be judged on screen
options.D: Either, because both produce identical information

questions.commentary: Physical prototypes are better for tactile qualities: weight, balance, texture and real spatial relationships. Virtual prototypes are better for rapid iteration, performance simulation and sharing between locations. The two are complementary rather than alternatives, and most professional processes use both.

questions.subTitle: Physical Prototypes
questions.text: Which of the following is a disadvantage of physical prototypes compared with virtual ones?

options.A: They cannot be evaluated by non-technical reviewers
options.B: They cannot be used for user testing
options.C: They cannot show the proportions of a large product
options.D: Modifying one often means rebuilding it, and extreme conditions are hard to test

questions.commentary: A physical prototype has to be remade to be changed, while a virtual model can be modified and re-tested in minutes, and simulations can apply crash or thermal loads that would destroy a physical model. Physical prototypes remain the better option for tangibility, which is exactly why designers narrow the options virtually first.

questions.subTitle: Physical Prototypes
questions.text: A foam model is shaped and painted to match the intended finish of a product but contains no working parts. It is best described as:

options.A: A functional prototype
options.B: An aesthetic model
options.C: A full-scale working prototype
options.D: A scale model

questions.commentary: Aesthetic models are accurate in appearance but not necessarily functional, and are used for visual evaluation, stakeholder presentation and photography. A functional prototype tests whether the product works and may look nothing like the final object, while a full-scale working prototype combines both and is used for final testing and approval.

questions.subTitle: Virtual Prototypes
questions.text: Which statement describes generative design?

options.A: The designer supplies loads, constraints and a goal, and the software generates and tests candidate geometries
options.B: The designer describes a product in ordinary language and the software models what was described
options.C: The software records how a user moves and maps that data onto a digital model
options.D: The software overlays a digital model onto a view of the real environment

questions.commentary: In generative design the designer defines the problem rather than the shape: preserved and obstacle geometry, load cases, material and manufacturing method, and a goal such as minimum weight. The software then generates, stress-tests and refines candidate shapes and returns many options to compare. Describing a model in words is agentic modelling, which builds what you asked for without optimising anything.

questions.subTitle: Virtual Prototypes
questions.text: Finite element analysis (FEA) is most commonly used to simulate:

options.A: The colour and surface texture of a product
options.B: The likely market demand for a product
options.C: How stress, strain and temperature distribute through a structure under load
options.D: The assembly sequence used by factory workers

questions.commentary: FEA divides the model into a mesh of thousands of small elements and calculates how stress, strain, displacement and temperature spread through the structure when forces are applied. The colour-coded output shows where a part would deform or fail, which is what allows crash performance and fatigue life to be assessed before anything is built.

questions.subTitle: Virtual Prototypes
questions.text: A designer wants to test how stiff a new car door latch will feel to the hand before any physical prototype exists. Which technology is most appropriate?

options.A: Finite element analysis
options.B: Orthographic projection
options.C: Augmented reality
options.D: Haptic technology

questions.commentary: Haptic devices deliver force feedback through a controller or glove, so a designer can feel simulated resistance from a virtual mechanism. FEA reports stress rather than sensation, orthographic drawings communicate dimensions, and augmented reality shows how something looks in a real setting rather than how it feels.

questions.subTitle: Rapid Prototyping
questions.text: Which rapid prototyping technology cures liquid photopolymer resin layer by layer using UV light?

options.A: Fused deposition modelling (FDM)
options.B: Stereolithography (SLA)
options.C: Selective laser sintering (SLS)
options.D: CNC milling

questions.commentary: SLA cures liquid photopolymer resin in layers of roughly 0.05 to 0.15 mm, giving the smoothest finish of the three additive processes, though the parts are brittle and need washing and UV curing afterwards. FDM extrudes melted filament, SLS sinters powder, and CNC milling is subtractive rather than additive.

questions.subTitle: Rapid Prototyping
questions.text: Selective laser sintering (SLS) differs from fused deposition modelling (FDM) mainly because SLS:

options.A: Uses liquid resin rather than powder
options.B: Can only produce metal parts
options.C: Needs no separate support structures, because unsintered powder supports each layer
options.D: Produces a smoother surface finish than any other process

questions.commentary: The unsintered powder surrounding the part supports every layer, so overhangs and even interlocking moving parts can be built in one go. FDM needs printed supports for overhangs, which must be removed and leave marks. SLA, not SLS, gives the smoothest finish, and SLS parts must cool slowly to avoid warping.

questions.subTitle: Classifying Materials
questions.text: Corrosion resistance is classified as a chemical property rather than a physical one because it:

options.A: Can only be measured in a laboratory
options.B: Depends on the density of the material
options.C: Changes with the temperature of the material
options.D: Involves a chemical reaction between the material and another substance

questions.commentary: Physical properties such as density, melting point and thermal conductivity describe what a material is and can be measured without changing it. Chemical properties describe what a material does when it meets another substance, and the reaction alters its composition. Mechanical properties describe what it can withstand under force.

questions.subTitle: Material Categories
questions.text: Which statement about the three polymer groups is correct?

options.A: Thermosets can be remelted and reshaped repeatedly
options.B: Thermoplastics can be remelted and reshaped, while thermosets are permanently cross-linked
options.C: Elastomers cannot return to their original shape once deformed
options.D: All three groups occur naturally rather than being human-made

questions.commentary: Thermoplastics such as polyethylene, polypropylene, ABS and PET soften on heating and can be reshaped, which is what makes them recyclable by remelting. Thermosets such as epoxy and polyester resin cross-link permanently during curing and cannot be remelted. Elastomers such as rubber and silicone are flexible and do return to shape.

questions.subTitle: Material Selection
questions.text: A designer plots stiffness against density on an Ashby chart and marks out the region above 50 GPa and below 3000 kg/m³. The purpose of doing this is to:

options.A: Turn a list of requirements into a visual shortlist of candidate material families
options.B: Calculate the manufacturing cost of the finished product
options.C: Determine the melting point of each candidate material
options.D: Confirm that the chosen material will biodegrade

questions.commentary: Each material family occupies a bubble on the chart rather than a single point, because properties vary with processing and composition. Drawing a target zone shows at a glance which families fall inside it, reducing dozens of candidates to a handful worth investigating in detail. Cost, processing and sustainability are then weighed separately.

questions.subTitle: Physical Properties
questions.text: A steel rod is heated from 20°C to 300°C. Which physical property determines how much it will grow in length?

options.A: Density
options.B: Thermal conductivity
options.C: Coefficient of thermal expansion
options.D: Electrical resistivity

questions.commentary: The coefficient of thermal expansion gives the fractional change in length per degree of temperature change, so it predicts how far the rod grows. For mild steel it is about 11 × 10⁻⁶ K⁻¹, which is why bridges need expansion joints and pipelines need flexible connectors. Thermal conductivity describes how fast heat travels through the material, not how much it expands.

questions.subTitle: Chemical Properties
questions.text: Which statement best explains why stainless steel resists corrosion while mild steel does not?

options.A: Stainless steel contains no iron
options.B: Chromium forms a thin, stable oxide layer that reseals itself if scratched
options.C: Stainless steel does not react with oxygen at all
options.D: Stainless steel has a much lower melting point

questions.commentary: This is passivation. Chromium reacts with oxygen to form a chromium oxide layer only nanometres thick, which blocks further oxidation and reforms when damaged. Mild steel does not passivate: it forms loose, flaky rust that keeps exposing fresh metal, so degradation continues.

questions.subTitle: Mechanical Properties
questions.text: A material with a high Young's modulus is characterised by:

options.A: High toughness, meaning it absorbs a lot of energy before fracture
options.B: High ductility, meaning it can be drawn into wire
options.C: A low melting point
options.D: High stiffness, meaning it deflects very little under load

questions.commentary: Young's modulus is the ratio of stress to strain in the elastic region, so a high value means the material resists elastic deformation. Steel is around 200 GPa while rubber is under 0.1 GPa. Stiffness is not the same as strength or toughness: a very stiff material can still be brittle and fracture at a low load.

questions.subTitle: Mechanical Properties
questions.text: Which hardness test uses a steel or tungsten carbide ball and is best suited to castings and other inhomogeneous structures?

options.A: Vickers
options.B: Durometer
options.C: Brinell
options.D: Janka

questions.commentary: Brinell presses a ball into the surface and leaves a comparatively wide indentation, which averages out local variation in the structure. Vickers uses a diamond pyramid and suits metals and ceramics that need comparable values, Durometer is for polymers and elastomers, and Janka is used for timber.

questions.subTitle: Composites
questions.text: Which of the following is a particle-reinforced composite?

options.A: Concrete, gravel held in a cement matrix
options.B: Carbon fibre reinforced plastic
options.C: Plywood
options.D: Laminated glass

questions.commentary: Concrete is hard particles distributed through a softer matrix, which is the definition of a particle-reinforced composite, as is cemented carbide. CFRP is fibre-reinforced, while plywood and laminated glass are laminar composites built from bonded layers.

questions.subTitle: Smart Materials
questions.text: A coronary stent is inserted in a compressed form and opens to a pre-set diameter once it reaches body temperature. The material responsible is:

options.A: A piezoelectric ceramic
options.B: A shape memory alloy
options.C: A photochromic polymer
options.D: A magneto-rheostatic fluid

questions.commentary: Shape memory alloys such as Nitinol return to a pre-programmed shape when heated after being deformed at a lower temperature, which is what lets a stent be delivered through a catheter and expand inside the artery. Piezoelectric materials respond to mechanical stress or voltage, photochromic materials to UV light, and magneto-rheostatic fluids to a magnetic field.

questions.subTitle: Biodegradable Materials
questions.text: A cup moulded from PLA is labelled "compostable". Which statement is correct?

options.A: It will break down in a domestic compost bin within a few weeks
options.B: It is chemically identical to conventional polyethylene
options.C: It needs industrial composting conditions, so in landfill it behaves much like ordinary plastic
options.D: It can be recycled alongside conventional plastics without sorting

questions.commentary: PLA is derived from crop starch and does biodegrade, but only under sustained high temperature and the microbial conditions of an industrial composting facility. Where those facilities do not exist, the product is landfilled and the environmental benefit is not realised, which is why a biodegradable specification has to be matched to a real end-of-life pathway and clear disposal instructions.

questions.subTitle: Structures in nature & built environment
questions.text: A long bone is a hollow tube of dense cortical bone surrounding a lattice of spongy bone. The structural advantage of this arrangement is that it:

options.A: Removes any need for the bone to resist compression
options.B: Keeps material where bending stress is greatest while keeping overall mass low
options.C: Makes the bone stronger in tension than in compression
options.D: Allows the bone to change shape under load

questions.commentary: In bending, stress is greatest at the outer surfaces and close to zero at the centre, so material near the axis contributes little. A hollow tube places the dense material where it does the work, which is the same reasoning behind hollow tubes and I-sections in engineered structures. Honeycombs and eggshells solve the equivalent problem for compression using geometry rather than mass.

questions.subTitle: Structure classification
questions.text: A concrete dam is an example of which type of structure?

options.A: Solid structure
options.B: Frame structure
options.C: Shell structure
options.D: Combination structure

questions.commentary: A dam resists load through the bulk and mass of a continuous dense material, which is the defining feature of a solid structure. A frame carries load through a skeleton of connected members, and a shell through a thin curved surface. Solid structures suit situations where weight is not a constraint and forces arrive from unpredictable directions.

questions.subTitle: Structural members
questions.text: Which structural member is fixed at one end only, with the other end projecting freely?

options.A: Simply supported beam
options.B: Fixed beam
options.C: Continuously supported beam
options.D: Cantilever beam

questions.commentary: A cantilever resists the entire bending moment at its single fixed end, which is why the root of a diving board or an aircraft wing is the most heavily loaded point and needs a rigid fixing. A simply supported beam rests freely on two supports, a fixed beam is built in at both ends, and a continuously supported beam spans more than two supports.

questions.subTitle: Static and dynamic forces
questions.text: A car drive shaft transmitting torque from the engine to the wheels is loaded mainly in:

options.A: Compression
options.B: Tension
options.C: Torsion
options.D: Shear

questions.commentary: Torsion twists a member about its own longitudinal axis, which is exactly what a drive shaft does while transmitting torque. Compression squashes, tension stretches, and shear makes adjacent layers slide past one another. Most real members carry a combination: a drill bit, for example, is in torsion and compression at the same time.

questions.subTitle: Stress, strain and Young's Modulus
questions.text: On a stress-strain graph, the yield strength is the stress at which:

options.A: The material fractures completely
options.B: Permanent plastic deformation begins
options.C: Stress and strain first become proportional
options.D: Strain returns to zero on unloading

questions.commentary: Below the yield point deformation is elastic and the material springs back; above it a permanent set remains after unloading. The ultimate tensile strength is the peak of the curve, where necking begins, and fracture is the final break. In brittle materials the curve drops away steeply from near the UTS with little plastic deformation in between.

questions.subTitle: Young's Modulus in material selection
questions.text: Which application calls for a material with a deliberately low Young's modulus?

options.A: An engine mount that must absorb vibration
options.B: A bridge deck where deflection must be minimised
options.C: An aircraft wing spar
options.D: A shelf that must not sag under load

questions.commentary: A low modulus means large elastic deformation for a small load, which is what allows rubber and soft polymers to absorb energy and vibration, seal joints and cushion fragile contents. High modulus materials such as steel, titanium and CFRP are chosen wherever geometry must be held precisely under load.

questions.subTitle: Equilibrium and structural failure
questions.text: A structure is in static equilibrium when:

options.A: It is moving at constant velocity
options.B: It is carrying its maximum design load
options.C: Its safety factor is exactly 1
options.D: The sum of all forces is zero and the sum of all moments is zero

questions.commentary: Both conditions are required. Forces summing to zero stops the structure translating, and moments summing to zero stops it rotating. If the forces balance but the moments do not, the structure turns rather than stays still.

questions.subTitle: Strengthening techniques
questions.text: An I-beam resists bending efficiently because:

options.A: It is formed from a single metal crystal
options.B: Its material is stiffer than that of a solid rectangular bar
options.C: The flanges place material where bending stress is greatest, while the thin web carries shear
options.D: It is always manufactured from aluminium

questions.commentary: Bending stress peaks at the top and bottom faces and falls to near zero at the neutral axis, so material near the centre earns very little. Moving material outwards raises the second moment of area, because each element counts in proportion to the square of its distance from the axis. Two beams of identical steel can therefore differ greatly in bending stiffness purely through shape.

questions.subTitle: Safety factors: definition
questions.text: A footbridge has a maximum expected service load of 10,000 N and fails at 25,000 N. Its safety factor is:
questions.commentary: Safety factor is failure load divided by maximum service load, so 25,000 / 10,000 = 2.5. Public structures carry generous factors because real loads are uncertain, production material is weaker than laboratory specimens, structures degrade over decades, and the consequences of failure are severe.

questions.subTitle: Safety factors: typical values
questions.text: Aircraft structures are designed to safety factors of roughly 1.2 to 2, while lifting equipment uses 4 to 6. The main reason for the difference is that:

options.A: Aircraft loads are larger than crane loads
options.B: Aircraft materials never fatigue
options.C: Aircraft loads are tightly bounded and systems are redundant, while lifting loads are shock-prone with no redundancy
options.D: Lifting equipment is not designed for human safety

questions.commentary: Aircraft carry weight penalties for every extra kilogram, so the margin is kept tight and safety is bought instead through certified materials, strict operating envelopes, redundant systems and constant inspection. A crane cable has no redundancy and sees swinging, snatch loads and wear, so the margin has to be built into the structure itself. Over-engineering is not free: excess material costs energy, mass and sustainability.

questions.subTitle: Four types of motion
questions.text: A windscreen wiper sweeping back and forth across the glass is an example of:

options.A: Linear motion
options.B: Oscillating motion
options.C: Reciprocating motion
options.D: Rotary motion

questions.commentary: Oscillating motion is a back and forth movement along a curved arc about a fixed pivot, which is what a wiper, a pendulum and a swing all do. Reciprocating motion is also back and forth, but along a straight line, as in a piston or a sewing machine needle. That difference in path is the whole distinction.

questions.subTitle: Inputs, processes and outputs
questions.text: In a petrol engine, the connecting rod and crankshaft are best described as the:

options.A: Input
options.B: Output
options.C: Process
options.D: Load

questions.commentary: The input is the linear combustion force on the piston and the output is rotary motion at the crankshaft. The connecting rod and crank are the mechanism that transforms one into the other, which is the process stage of the input-process-output model. Identifying the required conversion is what tells a designer which mechanism family to reach for.

questions.subTitle: Mechanical advantage
questions.text: A ramp 2.5 m long raises a load to a height of 0.5 m. Its ideal mechanical advantage is:
questions.commentary: For an inclined plane, IMA is slope length divided by vertical height, so 2.5 / 0.5 = 5. The effort needed falls by a factor of five, but the load has to be pushed five times as far. Real machines fall short of this figure because of friction, which is the difference between ideal and actual mechanical advantage.

questions.subTitle: Changing speed, direction or power
questions.text: A small gear drives a larger gear. Compared with the input shaft, the output shaft has:

options.A: Lower speed and greater torque
options.B: Higher speed and greater torque
options.C: Lower speed and lower torque
options.D: Higher speed and the same torque

questions.commentary: At constant power, speed and torque are always traded against one another. A 20-tooth gear driving a 40-tooth gear gives a ratio of 2:1, so the output turns at half the speed with roughly double the torque. It is the same bargain as the inclined plane: gain force, lose distance.

questions.subTitle: Combining motion types
questions.text: A manual can opener combines which three simple machines?

options.A: Pulley, screw and inclined plane
options.B: Lever, pulley and screw
options.C: Lever, wedge and wheel and axle
options.D: Screw, linkage and cam

questions.commentary: The handles act as levers to grip the can and multiply force, the cutting wheel is a wedge that shears the lid, and the turning handle is a wheel and axle that drives the cutter around the rim. Complex mechanisms are analysed this way throughout: follow the chain from input to output and name the conversion happening at each stage.

questions.subTitle: Gear systems
questions.text: Adding an idler gear between a driving gear and a driven gear:

options.A: Changes the speed ratio between input and output
options.B: Reverses the direction of rotation of the output without changing the ratio
options.C: Increases torque while holding speed constant
options.D: Removes the need for lubrication

questions.commentary: An idler adds and then removes the same term from the ratio calculation, so speed and torque are unaffected. Its jobs are to reverse the output direction and to let the driving and driven shafts sit further apart. An odd number of idlers returns the original direction, an even number reverses it.

questions.subTitle: Belt and chain drives
questions.text: The fundamental difference between a belt drive and a chain drive is that:

options.A: A belt transmits power through friction, while a chain transmits it by meshing with sprocket teeth
options.B: A chain drive is quieter than a belt drive
options.C: A belt drive carries heavier loads than a chain drive
options.D: A chain drive requires no maintenance

questions.commentary: Friction transmission means a belt can slip under overload, which loses precision but can protect the machine. A chain interlocks positively with the sprocket, so the ratio is exact and heavy loads can be carried, at the cost of noise, weight and the need for lubrication. Toothed synchronous belts are the exception, meshing rather than gripping, which is why timing belts use them.

questions.subTitle: Cams
questions.text: Which cam profile produces a slow, gradual rise followed by a sudden drop?

options.A: Circular (eccentric) cam
options.B: Pear cam
options.C: Oval cam
options.D: Snail cam

questions.commentary: The snail or drop cam lifts the follower gradually around the spiral and then releases it abruptly at the foot, which is how trip hammers and alarm clock strikers work. A circular cam gives smooth continuous rise and fall with no dwell, a pear cam holds the follower still for most of a revolution before a quick rise and fall, and an oval cam gives two cycles per revolution.

questions.subTitle: Levers
questions.text: Rising onto the balls of the feet uses the foot as which class of lever?

options.A: First class
options.B: Second class
options.C: Third class
options.D: No lever is involved

questions.commentary: The joint at the ball of the foot is the fulcrum, body weight acts at the ankle as the load, and the calf muscles pull on the heel as the effort. Load between fulcrum and effort makes this second class, so the effort arm is always longer and mechanical advantage is always above 1. Most other body levers are third class, trading force for speed and range.

questions.subTitle: Linkages
questions.text: Squeezing the handles of a pair of bolt cutters drives the jaws together, so input and output move in opposite directions. This is:

options.A: A parallel linkage
options.B: A bell-crank linkage
options.C: A reverse linkage
options.D: A rack and pinion

questions.commentary: A reverse linkage pivots about a central point so that the output travels opposite to the input, as in bolt cutters, locking pliers and brake pedal linkages. A parallel linkage keeps the output moving in the same direction and orientation, as in a scissor lift or a desk lamp arm, and a bell crank redirects motion through roughly 90 degrees.

questions.subTitle: Input-Process-Output model
questions.text: In the IPO model of an electronic system, which stage receives the sensor signal and decides on an appropriate response?

options.A: Input
options.B: Process
options.C: Output
options.D: Feedback

questions.commentary: The process stage, whether a microcontroller, logic circuit or op-amp, applies the system's rules to the incoming signal and determines what the output should do. The input converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal, the output converts the decision back into a physical effect, and feedback returns information about the result so the process can correct itself.

questions.subTitle: Electronics in everyday life
questions.text: EU regulations cap standby power at 0.5 W for most devices. This limit targets the power a product draws when it is:

options.A: Performing its main function at full load
options.B: Being manufactured and assembled
options.C: Connected to the supply but not in active use
options.D: Being recycled at end of life

questions.commentary: Standby loss, sometimes called phantom load, is the power consumed continuously by a device that is switched off or idle but still plugged in. Because it runs every hour of the product's life, small savings multiply across millions of units, which is why regulation targets it alongside in-use efficiency, restricted substances and design for disassembly.

questions.subTitle: Analogue signals and SI units
questions.text: Mains electricity in Australia is supplied at 230 V and 50 Hz. The period of one complete cycle is:

options.A: 20 ms
options.B: 50 ms
options.C: 5 ms
options.D: 230 ms

questions.commentary: Period is the reciprocal of frequency, so T = 1 / 50 = 0.02 s, which is 20 ms. The 230 V figure describes the voltage and plays no part in the calculation. Note the SI multiplier: milli means 10⁻³.

questions.subTitle: Digital signals and logic gates
questions.text: Which statement about NAND gates is correct?

options.A: The output is HIGH only when all inputs are HIGH
options.B: A NAND gate accepts only a single input
options.C: A NAND gate behaves identically to an XOR gate
options.D: NAND is a universal gate, so any logic function can be built from NAND gates alone

questions.commentary: NAND inverts the AND function, so its output is LOW only when every input is HIGH. Both NAND and NOR are universal, meaning adders, comparators, flip-flops and the rest of a processor's logic can be constructed from a single gate type. NOT is the gate with only one input, and XOR outputs HIGH when its inputs differ.

questions.subTitle: Electronic components
questions.text: The main function of a capacitor in a circuit is to:

options.A: Allow current to flow in one direction only
options.B: Store charge and energy in an electric field
options.C: Amplify a small signal into a larger one
options.D: Convert an electrical signal into movement

questions.commentary: A capacitor stores charge between its plates and releases it again, which is what makes it useful for smoothing a power supply, setting timing intervals and coupling or decoupling stages of a circuit. One-way conduction is a diode, amplification is a transistor or op-amp, and conversion to movement is an output transducer such as a motor or solenoid.

questions.subTitle: Input devices and sensors
questions.text: An NTC thermistor used as a temperature sensor behaves in which way?

options.A: Its resistance decreases as temperature rises
options.B: Its resistance increases as temperature rises
options.C: It emits light in proportion to temperature
options.D: Its resistance stays constant regardless of temperature

questions.commentary: NTC stands for negative temperature coefficient, so resistance falls as the device gets hotter. An LDR behaves similarly with light rather than heat. Knowing the direction of the change matters, because it determines how the sensor is arranged in a potential divider and which way the output voltage moves.

questions.subTitle: Output devices
questions.text: A microcontroller pin can supply roughly 40 mA. To drive a motor requiring 2 A, the designer must:

options.A: Connect the motor directly and reduce the supply voltage
options.B: Use thicker wire between the pin and the motor
options.C: Place a transistor, MOSFET driver or relay between the pin and the motor
options.D: Connect a capacitor in series with the motor

questions.commentary: The pin supplies only the small current needed to switch a driver, and the driver carries the load current from a separate supply. A relay adds electrical isolation as well, which is what allows a low-voltage microcontroller to switch a mains circuit safely. Connecting a high-current load directly to a pin destroys the microcontroller.

questions.subTitle: Feedback
questions.text: Negative feedback in a control system such as a thermostat acts to:

options.A: Amplify the difference between set point and actual output
options.B: Increase system gain without limit
options.C: Hold the output permanently at maximum
options.D: Reduce the difference between set point and actual output, making the system stable

questions.commentary: Negative feedback opposes the change in output, shrinking the error between the desired value and the actual one, which is what allows a thermostat or cruise control to settle rather than hunt. Positive feedback reinforces the change instead, producing the runaway squeal of a microphone near a speaker, though it is used deliberately in oscillators and Schmitt triggers.

questions.subTitle: Operational amplifiers
questions.text: An inverting amplifier is built with R₁ = 2 kΩ and R₂ = 20 kΩ. Its voltage gain is:
questions.commentary: For an inverting amplifier the gain is −R₂/R₁, so −20 kΩ / 2 kΩ = −10. The minus sign means the output is inverted relative to the input, not that it is smaller. The same resistors in a non-inverting configuration would give 1 + R₂/R₁ = +11.

questions.subTitle: Circuit diagrams
questions.text: Which statement about a parallel circuit is correct?

options.A: The same current flows through every component
options.B: Total resistance is the sum of the branch resistances
options.C: Every branch has the same voltage across it, and total resistance is lower than the smallest branch
options.D: If one branch goes open circuit, the whole circuit stops working

questions.commentary: Parallel branches share the same two nodes, so they share a voltage while the current divides between them, and adding branches lowers the total resistance. Series circuits are the opposite case: one path, the same current everywhere, resistances that add, and total failure if any component goes open. Household wiring is parallel for exactly this reason.

questions.subTitle: Five categories
questions.text: Which description best fits an additive manufacturing process?

options.A: Building an object layer by layer from a digital model
options.B: Removing material from a solid block with a rotating cutter
options.C: Reshaping material by forcing it into a mould
options.D: Bonding two components with a filler alloy

questions.commentary: Additive processes deposit or cure material one cross-section at a time, placing material only where it is needed. Removing material is subtractive, reshaping without adding or removing is forming, and bonding parts together is joining. Most real products need techniques from several categories in sequence.

questions.subTitle: Additive techniques
questions.text: FDM parts are described as anisotropic because:

options.A: They absorb moisture from the surrounding air
options.B: The filament changes composition as it is heated
options.C: The nozzle deposits a different material on every pass
options.D: Each layer bonds only partially to the one above, so the part is weaker across the layer lines

questions.commentary: Anisotropic means the mechanical properties depend on the direction of loading. An FDM part is well fused within each layer but only partly fused between layers, so it fails more readily when pulled apart in the build direction. This is why print orientation is a design decision, not just a setup detail.

questions.subTitle: Rapid prototyping
questions.text: Which of these is characteristic of a rapid prototype rather than a production part?

options.A: Manufactured in the specified engineering material to full tolerance
options.B: One to five units in a cheap polymer, made to test geometry, fit and ergonomics
options.C: Produced in runs of hundreds of thousands of identical units
options.D: Requires dedicated tooling before the first part can exist

questions.commentary: Rapid prototypes trade material specification and finish for speed, going from CAD to a physical model in hours with no tooling. Production parts justify tooling cost and longer lead times because it is amortised across volume. The boundary is blurring as additive materials improve, with certified additive parts such as the LEAP engine fuel nozzle now in service.

questions.subTitle: 4D printing
questions.text: In 4D printing with a shape memory polymer, the "programming" stage involves:

options.A: Cooling the part to cryogenic temperature to lock it rigid
options.B: Cross-linking the polymer permanently with UV light
options.C: Heating above the glass transition temperature, deforming the part, then cooling to fix a temporary shape
options.D: Soaking the part in water so that it swells into the required form

questions.commentary: The part is printed in its permanent shape, programmed into a temporary one above the glass transition temperature, fixed by cooling below it, and later triggered by a stimulus so it recovers the printed geometry. The fourth dimension is time, since the transformation happens after printing. Self-deploying stents triggered by body heat are the standard biomedical example.

questions.subTitle: 5D printing
questions.text: The two additional rotational axes used in 5D additive manufacturing allow the machine to:

options.A: Deposit material along curved paths, removing the need for supports and giving more uniform strength
options.B: Print without needing a CAD model
options.C: Print two different materials at the same time
options.D: Cure thermoset resins without any heat or light

questions.commentary: Rotating the head and the bed keeps the nozzle at a workable angle to the surface, so overhangs no longer need support material and the deposited lines can follow the stress paths through the part. That gives less waste, a larger effective build volume and strength closer to isotropic, which is why the process suits curved skull implants and load-bearing automotive brackets.

questions.subTitle: Subtractive techniques
questions.text: Abrasive waterjet cutting is chosen in preference to laser cutting mainly because it:

options.A: Requires no computer control
options.B: Produces no waste material at all
options.C: Is the only process capable of cutting sheet metal
options.D: Cuts hard and heat-sensitive materials without a heat-affected zone

questions.commentary: A waterjet cuts by erosion using water at 280 to 690 MPa carrying abrasive grit, so it introduces no heat into the workpiece and will cut stone, glass, titanium and composites that a laser would melt, char or distort. All subtractive processes generate waste in the form of swarf, chips or spent abrasive.

questions.subTitle: Forming techniques
questions.text: Continuous casting of steel belongs to which manufacturing category?

options.A: Additive
options.B: Subtractive
options.C: Forming
options.D: Joining

questions.commentary: Forming reshapes material without adding or removing any of it, exploiting plasticity or the fluidity of a molten state. Continuous casting solidifies molten steel into a strand in a water-cooled copper mould, and its output is stock material for later processing rather than a finished component. Because nothing is wasted, forming is generally more material-efficient than subtractive methods.

questions.subTitle: Joining techniques
questions.text: A designer specifies mechanical fasteners rather than adhesive bonding for a product's outer casing. The main advantage of this decision is that:

options.A: Fasteners are always lighter than an adhesive joint
options.B: The joint can be undone, allowing repair, part replacement and end-of-life disassembly
options.C: Fasteners can join dissimilar materials while adhesives cannot
options.D: Fasteners create a permanent joint that cannot be tampered with

questions.commentary: Bolts, screws, snap-fits and cam locks are temporary joints, so the assembly can be opened for repair and separated into material streams for recycling. Welding, soldering, brazing and adhesives all make permanent joints, which is faster and often lighter but closes off both repair and material recovery. IKEA's cam lock is the classic example of a reversible joint chosen deliberately.

questions.subTitle: Finishing techniques
questions.text: Steel street furniture is hot-dip galvanised rather than painted mainly because the zinc coating:

options.A: Grows into the surface of the steel as an oxide layer
options.B: Can be applied to polymers and timber as well as steel
options.C: Is applied without heat, so the steel is not distorted
options.D: Corrodes in preference to the steel, so protection continues even where the surface is scratched

questions.commentary: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it gives sacrificial cathodic protection: the coating is consumed first and the steel underneath survives even where the surface has been damaged. Dipping in molten zinc at around 450 °C also gives a much thicker layer than paint or plating. Anodising, by contrast, grows an oxide layer into the surface but works on aluminium rather than steel.

questions.subTitle: Combining techniques
questions.text: Why does injection moulding become more cost-effective than FDM printing above roughly 10,000 units?

options.A: The one-off tooling cost is spread across every part made, so the per-unit cost falls with volume
options.B: Injection moulding uses less electricity per part at every volume
options.C: FDM cannot process engineering-grade thermoplastics
options.D: Moulded parts are stronger than printed parts in every direction

questions.commentary: Injection moulding pairs a very high tooling cost with a very low cost and cycle time per part, so the per-unit figure falls steeply as volume rises. Additive manufacturing has almost no setup cost but a roughly constant cost per part, which is why it wins for low volumes, high complexity and customised parts such as patient-specific implants.

questions.subTitle: UCD Planning
questions.text: Which is the strongest research question for a UCD plan aimed at improving a ride-sharing app?

options.A: "Should the app have a dark mode?"
options.B: "How many buttons should the home screen have?"
options.C: "At what point during a ride request do users feel most uncertain, and why?"
options.D: "What colour scheme do users prefer?"

questions.commentary: Strong research questions are about behaviour, frustration and motivation, and they name something you do not yet know about your users. The others are feature decisions, which can only be answered sensibly once the underlying user need is understood, so asking them first tends to confirm what the team had already decided to build.

questions.subTitle: UCD Planning
questions.text: A cordless drill is being redesigned for two groups: tradespeople who use it daily and occasional DIY users. Which approach best exposes where their priorities diverge?

options.A: A single focus group containing both groups together
options.B: Structured interviews with each group separately, using the same set of questions
options.C: A Likert survey issued to professionals only
options.D: Observation of DIY users at home only

questions.commentary: Identical questions asked of each group separately give directly comparable answers, so any divergence in priorities, such as battery endurance and fast bit changes against ease of learning and storage, shows up clearly. Mixing the groups risks one set of voices dominating, and sampling only one group cannot reveal a difference at all.

questions.subTitle: Research Methods
questions.text: Which method is best suited to revealing the gap between what users say they do and what they actually do?

options.A: Structured interview
options.B: Likert scale questionnaire
options.C: Focus group
options.D: Field research

questions.commentary: Field research puts the researcher into the kitchen, bus or workshop where the product is really used, exposing workarounds and habits so automatic that no participant would report them. Its costs are time and the observer effect. Interviews, questionnaires and focus groups all rely on what people choose to tell you.

questions.subTitle: Research Methods
questions.text: A researcher watching factory workers sees every step of a safety check performed correctly, although records suggest steps are normally skipped. This is best explained by:

options.A: The observer effect
options.B: Cognitive load
options.C: Poka-yoke
options.D: The method of extremes

questions.commentary: People change their behaviour when they know they are being watched, so observational data is a mixture of normal and watched behaviour. Researchers reduce the effect by running longer sessions so the novelty fades, using passive sources such as analytics or logs, and triangulating observations against a separate interview or questionnaire.

questions.subTitle: Personae
questions.text: The primary purpose of building a persona is to:

options.A: Remove the need for user testing later in the process
options.B: Represent a user group with shared goals, so designs can be tested against real requirements
options.C: Record the exact height and weight of one real user
options.D: Identify the cheapest available manufacturing method

questions.commentary: A persona is a composite drawn from patterns across many users, not a single individual and not the designer's imagination. Its value lies in specificity: concrete frustrations, real limits and a defined use scenario let a team settle design arguments by asking whether this person could actually complete the task.

questions.subTitle: Personae
questions.text: An anti-persona is best described as:

options.A: A persona representing the most loyal customer
options.B: The average participant in a focus group
options.C: A user group that could misuse the product in ways that harm real users or the business
options.D: A fictional character used only in advertising

questions.commentary: Designing with an anti-persona in mind surfaces security gaps, safety issues and abuse routes before launch rather than after. They are not always hostile: a booking site that knows many visitors will never buy a ticket still designs a good experience for them, and a fast food chain uses anti-personae to avoid targeting customers its products cannot serve.

questions.subTitle: Usability
questions.text: A user returns to an app after six months away and completes a task without needing to relearn it. Which usability objective does this demonstrate?

options.A: Learnability
options.B: Efficiency
options.C: Errors
options.D: Memorability

questions.commentary: Memorability is how easily proficiency returns after a period of not using the product, the reason most adults can ride a bicycle again within minutes. Learnability concerns the very first use, efficiency the speed of a practised user, and errors how often mistakes happen and how easily they are recovered. All five objectives should be evaluated together.

questions.subTitle: Usability
questions.text: A battery compartment is shaped so that a cell physically cannot be inserted the wrong way round. This is an example of:

options.A: Poka-yoke, addressing the errors objective
options.B: The method of extremes, addressing percentile range
options.C: A use case, addressing satisfaction
options.D: Task analysis, addressing efficiency

questions.commentary: Poka-yoke, or mistake-proofing, makes the error impossible rather than warning the user after it happens. Fuel nozzles sized so diesel cannot enter a petrol filler, microwave doors that cut power the moment they open and reversible USB-C plugs all work the same way, designing the failure out instead of labelling it.

questions.subTitle: Task Analysis
questions.text: Hierarchical task analysis (HTA) works by:

options.A: Measuring brain activity while a user performs a task
options.B: Breaking an overall goal into sub-goals, operations and plans until each step is an action a user can perform
options.C: Recording physical movement only, ignoring the structure of the task
options.D: Replacing user testing with a mathematical model

questions.commentary: HTA maps the structure of a task so that hesitation, error and abandonment can be located at a specific step. Cognitive task analysis is the companion method, mapping the knowledge and judgement the task demands rather than its structure, and the two are often used together because a complete picture needs both.

questions.subTitle: Task Analysis
questions.text: A task analysis of a mobile checkout finds that users are asked to create an account midway through entering their card details, and many abandon at that point. The problem is best described as:

options.A: Poor memorability
options.B: An anti-persona
options.C: A spike in cognitive load at the highest-friction step
options.D: The observer effect

questions.commentary: Cognitive load is the mental effort a step demands, and interrupting a task to make an unrelated decision pushes it up sharply, which is where users give up. The usual remedies are to split the step, add a visual cue or reduce the number of choices. Here the fix is to move account creation after order confirmation and offer it as an optional toggle.

questions.subTitle: Five-Phase Process
questions.text: Which statement best describes the five-phase design process?

options.A: It is iterative: designers cycle back to earlier phases as new information emerges
options.B: It is strictly linear, with each phase completed once and never revisited
options.C: It begins by presenting a solution and works backwards to the user
options.D: Ideation is completed before any user research is carried out

questions.commentary: Empathise, define, ideate and model, design a solution and present a solution describe an order of reasoning, not a one-way schedule. A prototype test that reveals an unexpected need sends the team back to empathising, and a material constraint can force the specification to be rewritten. A process that shows genuine changes of mind is stronger evidence than a straight line from problem to solution.

questions.subTitle: Research Overview
questions.text: During testing, a participant tells the designer that a handle "feels slippery when my hands are wet". This is:

options.A: Quantitative primary data
options.B: Quantitative secondary data
options.C: Qualitative primary data
options.D: Qualitative secondary data

questions.commentary: It is primary because the designer collected it first-hand, and qualitative because it describes an experience rather than a measurement. The quantitative counterpart would be a figure such as the percentage of users who dropped the product with wet hands. Good research uses both: the qualitative data explains the problem, the quantitative data measures progress against it.

questions.subTitle: Primary Research
questions.text: Which of the following is primary research?

options.A: Reading a textbook chapter on anthropometric data
options.B: Running your own user interviews and material tests
options.C: Analysing a competitor's published market report
options.D: Reviewing peer-reviewed journal articles

questions.commentary: The distinction is who collected the data and why. Primary data is gathered first-hand for your own question, which makes it authentic and context-specific but costly in time and access. Textbooks, market reports and journals are secondary: faster and cheaper, but collected for someone else's purpose and population.

questions.subTitle: User Journey Mapping
questions.text: A storyboard maps a user's journey frame by frame. Its main value to a designer is that it:

options.A: Provides the exact dimensions needed for manufacture
options.B: Removes the need to build prototypes
options.C: Records the psychographic profile of the user
options.D: Preserves the sequence and context of the journey, so pain points can be located and shared

questions.commentary: Each frame captures the user, their action, their environment and their emotional state, so friction is visible in context rather than as an isolated complaint. Every pain point identified this way is a design opportunity. It is the same logic as hierarchical task analysis: break the journey down far enough and the problem stops being vague.

questions.subTitle: Problem Statement
questions.text: Which of the following is a well-formed problem statement?

options.A: "We need to build a lightweight folding stool for hospitals."
options.B: "Users want a better product than the one they currently have."
options.C: "Nurses on twelve-hour ward shifts have nowhere to rest briefly during medication rounds, which increases fatigue and the risk of error."
options.D: "The product must cost under $40 and weigh under 2 kg."

questions.commentary: A problem statement names a specific user group, the difficulty they face, the context in which it happens and why it matters, without prescribing a solution. Beginning with "we need to build" states a solution before the problem has been defined, "users want a better product" names nobody in particular, and cost and mass limits belong in the specification.

questions.subTitle: Design Specifications
questions.text: In a design specification, a desirable criterion is one that:

options.A: Would improve the product, but can be traded off against cost or time
options.B: Must be met, or the design has failed
options.C: Is imposed by regulation and cannot be altered
options.D: Cannot be expressed in measurable terms

questions.commentary: Essential criteria are non-negotiable, and an idea that misses one cannot proceed. Desirable criteria are genuine improvements that may be sacrificed when they conflict with budget, schedule or a stronger requirement. Both should still be measurable, since a specification that cannot be tested cannot show whether an iteration succeeded.

questions.subTitle: Ideation Tools
questions.text: In the Six Thinking Hats method, which hat covers intuition, feelings and emotional response?

options.A: White hat
options.B: Red hat
options.C: Black hat
options.D: Green hat

questions.commentary: The red hat is the one mode where a gut reaction can be stated without having to justify it. White covers facts, black criticism, yellow optimism, green new ideas and blue the management of the process itself. Keeping the modes separate is what stops a group mixing criticism into the moment it is trying to generate ideas.

questions.subTitle: Iterative Evaluation
questions.text: A design matrix lists specifications as rows and competing ideas as columns, with a weighted score in each cell. Its main purpose is to:

options.A: Calculate the manufacturing cost of each idea
options.B: Generate additional ideas to evaluate
options.C: Produce the technical drawings needed for production
options.D: Make the trade-offs between ideas visible and defensible

questions.commentary: Scoring every idea against every specification forces the comparison to be explicit, so a decision can be defended when a stakeholder challenges it. It also pinpoints which aspects of a weaker idea need to change, which is far cheaper than building a full prototype and discovering the same thing afterwards.

questions.subTitle: Model-Test-Refine
questions.text: The PDSA cycle (plan, do, study, act) is best described as:

options.A: A single-pass process with no repetition
options.B: A continuous improvement loop matching the model, test and refine cycle
options.C: A marketing strategy used at product launch
options.D: A standard for laying out technical drawings

questions.commentary: Plan what to test, do it, study the data and act on what it showed, then start again better informed. Each loop reduces uncertainty, which is why a design that has been through several test and refine cycles fits real user needs far better than one developed in a single extended push.

questions.subTitle: Technical Drawings
questions.text: A technical drawing is labelled 1:10. This means that:

options.A: The drawing is ten times larger than the real object
options.B: Manufacturing tolerance is 10 mm
options.C: The real object is ten times larger than the drawing
options.D: Ten separate views are included on the sheet

questions.commentary: Scale is the ratio of drawing size to real size, so 1:10 means the object is ten times bigger than it appears on the sheet, and the scale must always be stated. Tolerances are annotated separately against individual dimensions, and orthographic projection conventionally shows three views rather than ten.

questions.subTitle: Drawing Types
questions.text: Which drawing style shows three faces of an object at once using 30 degree horizontal axes, keeping true dimensions along all three axes?

options.A: Isometric drawing
options.B: Orthographic projection
options.C: Perspective rendering
options.D: Exploded assembly drawing

questions.commentary: Isometric means equal measurement: nothing shrinks with distance, so a single image shows three faces without perspective distortion. That makes it readable by audiences without technical training, which is why it appears in presentations, patent illustrations and assembly manuals. A perspective rendering looks more realistic but no longer preserves true dimensions.

questions.subTitle: Drawing Types
questions.text: A manufacturer needs to produce a replacement part and requires exact dimensions, tolerances and material specifications. Which drawing should they be sent?

options.A: A perspective rendering
options.B: An isometric sketch
options.C: An orthographic engineering drawing
options.D: A photograph of the prototype

questions.commentary: Orthographic projection places front, top and side views perpendicular to their planes and carries the dimensions, tolerances and surface specifications production actually needs. The pictorial types communicate the idea convincingly but cannot be worked from, which is the point of matching the drawing to its audience.

questions.subTitle: Physical Prototypes
questions.text: A designer builds a rough cardboard model to check the proportions and layout of a product. This is best described as:

options.A: A high-fidelity aesthetic prototype
options.B: A low-fidelity aesthetic prototype
options.C: A low-fidelity functional prototype
options.D: A high-fidelity functional prototype

questions.commentary: Cardboard is a low-fidelity material and the question being asked is about form, proportion and space rather than whether anything works, so the prototype is aesthetic rather than functional. Dyson's cardboard models of the DC08 are the standard example of failing fast and cheaply before changes become expensive.

questions.subTitle: Physical Prototypes
questions.text: A team wants users to grip and lift a new kitchen tool for feedback, but the shape is still being refined. The most appropriate prototype is:

options.A: A conceptual sketch on paper
options.B: A high-fidelity functional prototype in the final materials
options.C: A low-fidelity aesthetic foam block
options.D: A medium-fidelity functional prototype using substitute materials

questions.commentary: Users must be able to hold and lift the object, so it has to function, but committing to final materials while the geometry is still moving would make every change expensive. Medium fidelity with substitute materials gives usable ergonomic feedback at a cost that still allows iteration.

questions.subTitle: CAD Models
questions.text: Which statement correctly distinguishes surface models from solid models?

options.A: Surface models can calculate mass and volume, while solid models cannot
options.B: Surface models define only the outer skin, while solid models enclose a volume
options.C: Surface models are always higher fidelity than solid models
options.D: Solid models cannot be exported for manufacture

questions.commentary: Because a surface model has nothing inside it, it cannot report mass, volume or centre of gravity, though it is excellent for the curvature quality of body panels and casings. A solid model encloses volume, which is what allows mass properties, mould-fill and toolpath simulation and direct export to FEA.

questions.subTitle: CAD Models
questions.text: Airbus produced its bionic cabin partition by supplying an algorithm with the load case, material, mounting points and a weight target, then comparing the geometries it returned. This approach is:

options.A: Finite element analysis
options.B: Surface modelling
options.C: Generative design
options.D: Rapid prototyping

questions.commentary: In generative design the designer defines the problem and the software explores the geometry, here producing a branching lattice no one would have drawn by hand that met the same certification load at 45% less mass. FEA tests a shape you already have, whereas generative design uses that same stress analysis inside a loop to produce candidate shapes.

questions.subTitle: Finite Element Analysis
questions.text: In an FEA result, yielding refers to the point at which:

options.A: Deformation stops being recoverable and a permanent change of shape remains
options.B: The model fails to export to STL format
options.C: The simulation exceeds available memory
options.D: Two components in an assembly interfere with each other

questions.commentary: Below the yield point the material springs back once the load is removed; above it a permanent set remains, which for most structural parts counts as failure even though nothing has broken. FEA also flags stress concentrations at holes and sharp corners, resolved with fillets, ribs or extra thickness, and predicts buckling in slender sections.

questions.subTitle: Finite Element Analysis
questions.text: An FEA plot shows a bracket well within its limits. What is the strongest reason to treat this result with caution?

options.A: FEA cannot be used on metal components
options.B: Colour contour plots carry no information
options.C: FEA always underestimates stress by a fixed amount
options.D: The result depends entirely on the mesh, material data and boundary conditions the analyst supplied

questions.commentary: Fix the bracket at one bolt hole instead of two, refine the mesh or change the material, and the same geometry returns a different answer. The software makes none of those choices, so "the simulation says it is fine" is a claim that should always be followed by questions about the assumptions behind it.

questions.subTitle: Rapid Prototyping
questions.text: Before a CAD model can be exported reliably for 3D printing, it must be:
