options.A: Built as a surface model with open edges
options.B: A watertight solid, with no gaps or self-intersecting geometry
options.C: Saved as a perspective rendering
options.D: Simplified until it contains only a handful of triangles

questions.commentary: An STL describes the shape as a mesh of flat triangles, so the model must enclose a volume cleanly for the slicer to know what is inside. Two further checks matter: enough triangles to keep curves and fine features from faceting away, and wall thicknesses above the minimum the process can build, which for a 0.4 mm FDM nozzle means around 1 mm in practice.

questions.subTitle: Prototypes & Feedback
questions.text: A client meeting has been called to approve the visual direction of a product before any functional development begins. The most appropriate model to bring is:

options.A: An orthographic drawing with full tolerances
options.B: An FEA stress contour plot
options.C: A perspective rendering or aesthetic presentation model
options.D: A breadboard prototype of the electronics

questions.commentary: Clients respond to appearance and to alignment with the brief, so a render or presentation model gathers exactly the reactions the meeting needs. Tolerance drawings and FEA outputs answer an engineer's or manufacturer's questions instead. Matching the model to the audience, rather than defaulting to the highest fidelity available, is what keeps iteration efficient.

questions.subTitle: Properties-based selection
questions.text: What is the first step in a material selection process?

options.A: Plotting the candidates on an Ashby chart
options.B: Choosing the manufacturing process
options.C: Defining the properties the product requires, from its use and operating conditions
options.D: Costing every material that could conceivably be used

questions.commentary: The required properties come from the operating environment, the performance the product must deliver and the failure modes to be avoided. Charts, processes and costs all follow from that. Choosing a material or a process first means working backwards from an assumption rather than from a requirement.

questions.subTitle: Properties-based selection
questions.text: Ashby charts plot material properties on logarithmic axes because:

options.A: Properties span many orders of magnitude, so a linear axis would hide most materials
options.B: Logarithmic scales remove the need to consider cost
options.C: Only logarithmic scales can display more than one material family
options.D: They convert every property into the same units

questions.commentary: Young's modulus runs from around 0.01 GPa for rubber to about 1000 GPa for diamond. On a linear axis nearly every material would be squashed against one end of the chart, so the comparison the chart exists to support would be impossible to read.

questions.subTitle: Properties-based selection
questions.text: A bicycle frame must resist flexing under pedalling and cornering loads while remaining as light as possible. Which performance index applies?

options.A: Specific strength, σₕ / ρ
options.B: Specific stiffness, E / ρ
options.C: Fracture toughness, Kⁱₓ
options.D: Thermal conductivity per unit cost, λ / Φ

questions.commentary: Resisting deflection is a stiffness problem, so the index is Young's modulus divided by density. Specific strength answers the different question of how much load a material can carry per unit mass before fracture, which matters for wing spars and chassis members. Steel has a high modulus but its density makes its specific stiffness relatively poor.

questions.subTitle: Properties-based selection
questions.text: A line of constant performance index drawn across an Ashby chart is called a:

options.A: Yield line
options.B: Fracture line
options.C: Property bubble
options.D: Design line

questions.commentary: Every material on a design line delivers the same performance for the chosen index, so for a maximisation problem everything above it performs better. Sliding the line upwards screens progressively fewer and better candidates, which is how a chart turns into a shortlist.

questions.subTitle: Aesthetic characteristics
questions.text: Which of the following is a functional finish rather than an aesthetic one?

options.A: Applied wood veneer
options.B: Galvanising for corrosion protection
options.C: Brushed stainless steel
options.D: Mirror polishing

questions.commentary: Galvanising is specified to extend service life, and any change in appearance is a side effect rather than the purpose. Veneer, brushing and polishing are chosen for how a product looks and feels. Heat treatment for hardness sits on the functional side for the same reason, and mixing the two categories is a common error in exam answers.

questions.subTitle: Aesthetic characteristics
questions.text: Car manufacturers deliberately engineer the solid sound a closing door makes. In material selection terms this is:

options.A: A functional finish
options.B: A manufacturability constraint
options.C: An aesthetic consideration, because sound shapes perceived quality
options.D: A sustainability criterion

questions.commentary: Aesthetic selection covers every sensory quality, not only appearance: colour, texture, form, sound and even smell. A dull thunk reads as solid and precise while a rattle reads as cheap, which is why panel mass and sealing materials are chosen partly for their acoustic effect. Premium headphone housings use dense materials for the same reason.

questions.subTitle: Cost, availability & sustainability
questions.text: Which statement best describes lifecycle cost?

options.A: Acquisition, processing, maintenance in service and end-of-life disposal or recovery combined
options.B: The raw material purchase price alone
options.C: The cost of the tooling required to form the material
options.D: The retail price paid by the customer

questions.commentary: A cheap material that needs regular re-treatment, or that is replaced twice over the same period, is not cheap. A stainless steel bottle costs more than a plastic one at the till but can be cheaper per use across ten years, and recyclable metals may even return value at end of life.

questions.subTitle: Cost, availability & sustainability
questions.text: Which of these is an example of availability, rather than manufacturability, influencing a material choice?

options.A: Titanium requires slower cutting speeds and specialist tooling
options.B: Thermosets cannot be remelted once cured
options.C: Some polymers can only be bonded with adhesive rather than welded
options.D: The required sheet thickness is not produced commercially, so another material is specified

questions.commentary: Availability covers whether the material can actually be obtained: local against global sourcing, renewable against finite supply, recyclability and the forms and section sizes that are commercially made. The other options all describe how easily the material can be shaped or joined, which is manufacturability.

questions.subTitle: Primary and secondary research
questions.text: Which of these is primary research in the context of material selection?

options.A: Reading a manufacturer's published data sheet
options.B: Running a salt spray corrosion test on candidate samples
options.C: Consulting an academic journal paper on fatigue in CFRP
options.D: Looking values up in an online property database

questions.commentary: Primary research generates first-hand data specific to the batch and condition in question: tensile, impact, hardness and corrosion tests, user reactions to material samples, and prototypes built from the candidate material. Data sheets, journals, standards and property databases are all secondary, gathered by others for their own purposes.

questions.subTitle: Primary and secondary research
questions.text: In a rigorous material selection report, how are the two research types normally combined?

options.A: Secondary research verifies the finalists while primary research screens the whole market
options.B: Secondary research replaces the need for primary research entirely
options.C: Secondary research screens many materials down to a shortlist, and primary research discriminates between the finalists in context
options.D: Primary research is used only to check regulatory compliance

questions.commentary: Charts and databases can reduce thousands of materials to a handful cheaply, but they describe idealised values rather than your batch, your process or your users. Testing the finalists yourself, and documenting the ranked criteria behind the decision, is what turns an assertion into a defensible justification.

questions.subTitle: Forces on structures
questions.text: Which stress is greatest at the outer surface of a shaft and falls to almost nothing at its centre, which is why hollow shafts are used?

options.A: Tension
options.B: Compression
options.C: Bending
options.D: Torsion

questions.commentary: Torsional stress increases with distance from the axis, so the core of a solid shaft carries very little load and mostly adds mass. Removing it gives nearly the same torsional strength at a much lower weight. Tension and compression, by contrast, are distributed uniformly across the cross-section.

questions.subTitle: Forces on structures
questions.text: A pin in a clevis joint carries its load across two shear planes. The shear stress in the pin is:

options.A: τ = F / A
options.B: τ = F / 2A
options.C: τ = 2F / A
options.D: τ = F / (πdt)

questions.commentary: With two planes resisting the load, each carries half of it, so the stress is halved compared with single shear. A single bolt joining two overlapping plates is the single shear case, and F / (πdt) is punching shear, where a punch is driven through a plate of thickness t.

questions.subTitle: Young's Modulus & stress-strain
questions.text: Young's modulus is defined as:

options.A: Force divided by cross-sectional area
options.B: Stress multiplied by strain
options.C: Stress divided by strain, taken within the elastic region
options.D: Strain divided by stress

questions.commentary: E is the gradient of the straight-line portion of the stress-strain graph, so a steeper slope means a stiffer material. Force divided by area is stress on its own. The value must be read from the elastic region, since beyond the yield point the relationship is no longer proportional.

questions.subTitle: Young's Modulus & stress-strain
questions.text: A test piece 50 mm long with a cross-sectional area of 20 mm² extends by 0.1 mm under a load of 80 kN. Young's modulus is:

options.A: 200 GPa
options.B: 2 GPa
options.C: 20 GPa
options.D: 400 GPa

questions.commentary: σ = F / A = 80,000 / 20 = 4,000 MPa, and ε = ΔL / L₀ = 0.1 / 50 = 0.002. Dividing gives E = 4,000 / 0.002 = 2,000,000 MPa, which is 200 GPa and consistent with steel. Working in newtons and mm² throughout keeps the result in MPa without any conversion.

questions.subTitle: Young's Modulus & stress-strain
questions.text: Aluminium, titanium and copper alloys show no clearly defined yield point on a stress-strain graph. Designers therefore quote:

options.A: Ultimate tensile strength instead
options.B: Proof stress, found by an offset of 0.2% strain
options.C: Fracture toughness
options.D: The elastic limit alone

questions.commentary: A line is drawn parallel to the elastic region but offset by 0.2% along the strain axis, and where it cuts the curve is the proof stress. This gives a usable design limit for materials whose transition from elastic to plastic behaviour is gradual rather than marked by a sudden drop in load.

questions.subTitle: Structural failure & FEA
questions.text: A long slender strut in compression suddenly deflects sideways and collapses at a load well below the compressive strength of its material. This failure mode is:

options.A: Necking
options.B: Punching shear
options.C: Buckling
options.D: Fatigue

questions.commentary: Euler showed that the critical buckling load depends on stiffness and geometry, Pₓₕ = π²EI / Lₑ², so doubling the effective length quarters the load a member can take. Hollow tubes and I-sections resist buckling better than solid rods of equal area because more material sits away from the centre. The Quebec Bridge's overloaded lower chords failed exactly this way.

questions.subTitle: Structural failure & FEA
questions.text: An FEA plot of a loaded plate is blue almost everywhere but shows a small red region around a drilled hole. The correct interpretation is that:

options.A: The entire plate is overloaded and the material must be changed
options.B: The mesh has failed to solve and the result should be discarded
options.C: The plate is too thick and should be reduced everywhere
options.D: The hole is a stress concentration, which can be eased with a larger fillet radius, a gusset or local thickening

questions.commentary: Stress concentrates at holes, notches and abrupt changes of section, and this is where fatigue cracks usually start. The large blue region carries the opposite message: material there is doing little work and could be removed to save weight, which is how FEA drives optimisation as well as safety checks.

questions.subTitle: Force diagrams
questions.text: The reaction at a roller support on a horizontal beam is:

options.A: Vertical only, perpendicular to the surface the roller rests on
options.B: Horizontal only
options.C: In any direction, with both vertical and horizontal components
options.D: A pure bending moment with no force

questions.commentary: A roller is free to move along the surface it sits on, so it cannot resist a horizontal force and contributes one unknown to the analysis. A pinned support resists in both directions and contributes two unknowns, while a fixed end also resists rotation, which is why a cantilever carries its maximum bending moment at the wall.

questions.subTitle: Force diagrams
questions.text: The maximum bending moment along a beam occurs where the shear force:

options.A: Reaches its largest value
options.B: Passes through zero
options.C: Is negative
options.D: Equals the dead load

questions.commentary: The bending moment diagram is the accumulated area under the shear force diagram, so the moment stops rising exactly where the shear crosses zero. That location is where the beam is most likely to fail in bending and therefore where the section must be sized.

questions.subTitle: Safety factors
questions.text: A steel rod of cross-sectional area 200 mm² has an ultimate tensile strength of 600 MPa and must be designed to a safety factor of 4. Its maximum working load is:

options.A: 7.5 kN
options.B: 120 kN
options.C: 30 kN
options.D: 480 kN

questions.commentary: Working stress is UTS divided by the safety factor, 600 / 4 = 150 MPa, and the load is that stress times the area, 150 × 200 = 30,000 N or 30 kN. Remember that the safety factor calculated at construction is not the one in service: the Morandi Bridge's corroded cables lost section for fifty years until the real factor fell below 1.

questions.subTitle: Mechanical Advantage
questions.text: A belt drive has a drive pulley of 100 mm diameter and a driven pulley of 300 mm. The mechanical advantage and its effect are:

options.A: MA = 0.33; the driven pulley turns three times faster with three times the torque
options.B: MA = 3; the driven pulley produces three times the torque and turns three times faster
options.C: MA = 0.33; the driven pulley produces one third of the torque at one third of the speed
options.D: MA = 3; the driven pulley produces three times the torque at one third of the speed

questions.commentary: MA is the ratio of driven to drive diameter, 300 / 100 = 3. Torque rises by that factor and speed falls by the same one, because power cannot be created by the mechanism. An input at 300 rpm would leave the driven pulley turning at 100 rpm.

questions.subTitle: Velocity Ratios
questions.text: In a crossed belt drive, the driven pulley:

options.A: Turns in the opposite direction to the drive pulley, with the ratio unchanged
options.B: Turns in the same direction as the drive pulley
options.C: Turns at twice the drive speed regardless of diameter
options.D: Only turns while the belt is slack

questions.commentary: Crossing the belt between the pulleys reverses the output direction without altering the diameters, so the speed and torque relationship is exactly as it would be with an open belt. An ordinary belt drive keeps both shafts turning the same way, whereas a meshing gear pair always reverses direction.

questions.subTitle: Velocity Ratios
questions.text: How is the overall ratio of a compound belt drive with two stages found?

options.A: By dividing the final pulley diameter by the first pulley diameter
options.B: By adding the two stage ratios
options.C: By multiplying the ratios of the individual stages together
options.D: By taking whichever stage ratio is larger

questions.commentary: Each stage passes its output on as the input to the next, so the ratios compound. Treating the arrangement as a single pair by comparing only the first and last pulley ignores the intermediate pair entirely and is one of the most common errors in this topic. The same rule applies to compound gear trains.

questions.subTitle: Efficiency
questions.text: In a belt drive, the effective force that transmits power is:

options.A: The tight side tension alone
options.B: The difference between the tight and slack side tensions
options.C: The slack side tension alone
options.D: The sum of the tight and slack side tensions

questions.commentary: Only the net difference in tension does useful work, so power transmitted is that difference multiplied by belt speed. The slack side still carries tension, which is what keeps the belt seated on the pulley, but it contributes nothing to the power delivered.

questions.subTitle: Efficiency
questions.text: A shaft transmits a torque of 1.8 N·m at 120 rpm. The power transmitted is approximately:
questions.commentary: Convert the speed first: ω = 120 × 2π / 60 = 12.57 rad/s. Then P = τω = 1.8 × 12.57 ≈ 22.6 W. Forgetting to convert rpm into rad/s is the usual source of a wrong answer here.

questions.subTitle: Gear & Belt Systems
questions.text: A compound gear train is chosen in preference to a simple gear train when:

options.A: A large speed or torque change is needed within a compact space
options.B: Cost is the only consideration
options.C: The two shafts must turn in the same direction
options.D: Only a single pair of gears is available

questions.commentary: Mounting two gears on a shared shaft lets each pair contribute its own ratio, and the ratios multiply. Achieving the same overall change with one pair would need a gear of impractical size, which is why gearboxes, drills and watches all use compound arrangements.

questions.subTitle: Gear & Belt Systems
questions.text: A 20-tooth gear drives a 60-tooth gear. On the same shaft as the 60-tooth gear sits a 15-tooth gear, which drives a 45-tooth gear. With an input speed of 900 rpm, the final output speed is:

options.A: 300 rpm
options.B: 100 rpm
options.C: 900 rpm
options.D: 8100 rpm

questions.commentary: Work stage by stage. The first pair gives 900 × 20 / 60 = 300 rpm, and because the second gear shares its shaft, that speed becomes the input to the second pair: 300 × 15 / 45 = 100 rpm. Each stage reduces speed by three, so the compact two-stage train achieves an overall reduction of nine.

questions.subTitle: Cams and Followers
questions.text: A cam follower stays at a constant height while the cam continues to rotate. This phase of the cam cycle is called:

options.A: Rise
options.B: Fall
options.C: Dwell
options.D: Stroke

questions.commentary: Dwell occurs wherever the cam radius stays constant, so the follower is held still. Rise and fall correspond to increasing and decreasing radius. Designing the sequence of rise, dwell and fall into the profile is how a camshaft controls how far an engine valve opens, for how long, and at what moment.

questions.subTitle: Levers
questions.text: A bicep curl, with the muscle attached to the forearm close to the elbow, is an example of:

options.A: A third-class lever that multiplies speed and range of movement
options.B: A first-class lever that multiplies force
options.C: A second-class lever that multiplies force
options.D: A pulley system rather than a lever

questions.commentary: The effort sits between the fulcrum and the load, so mechanical advantage is always below 1 and the muscle must exert far more force than the weight being lifted. What the body gains is range: a contraction of two or three centimetres sweeps the hand through some thirty-five, which is what makes throwing, writing and reaching possible.

questions.subTitle: Levers
questions.text: A 50 N load is held 0.35 m from the elbow. The bicep attaches 0.04 m from the joint and pulls at 75° to the forearm. The effort force required is approximately:
questions.commentary: Only the component perpendicular to the forearm creates a moment, so (E × sin 75°) × 0.04 = 50 × 0.35 = 17.5 N·m. That gives E = 17.5 / (0.966 × 0.04) ≈ 453 N. Omitting the sine term returns 437 N, which is the trap in this question.

questions.subTitle: Test Equipment
questions.text: A technician needs to measure the current flowing through one component of a live circuit. The correct method is a:

options.A: Multimeter connected in series, with the circuit broken to insert it
options.B: Multimeter connected in parallel across the component
options.C: Multimeter with the component removed from the circuit entirely
options.D: Oscilloscope probe connected across the component

questions.commentary: Current must flow through the meter, so the circuit has to be opened and the meter placed in the path. Connecting a current range in parallel short-circuits the component and can destroy the meter. Voltage is measured in parallel, and resistance only with the component removed from the circuit.

questions.subTitle: Test Equipment
questions.text: Which instrument is needed to diagnose ringing, the damped oscillation that follows a switching edge?

options.A: Digital multimeter
options.B: Clamp meter
options.C: Digital storage oscilloscope
options.D: Megohmmeter

questions.commentary: Ringing exists only in the time domain, so it needs an instrument that plots voltage against time. A multimeter returns a single number and would show nothing unusual, a clamp meter reads current magnitude, and a megohmmeter tests insulation resistance on a circuit that is not live.

questions.subTitle: V, I, R and P
questions.text: A 12 V supply is connected across a 470 Ω resistor. The power dissipated is approximately:
questions.commentary: Using P = V² / R avoids an intermediate step: 144 / 470 = 0.306 W. Working the long way gives the same result, since I = V / R = 25.5 mA and P = VI = 12 × 0.0255 = 0.306 W. The 25.5 figure is the current in milliamps, not the power.

questions.subTitle: Resistors & Capacitors
questions.text: Two 100 Ω resistors in parallel are connected in series with a 50 Ω resistor. The total resistance is:
questions.commentary: Resolve the parallel branch first: two equal resistors give R / n = 100 / 2 = 50 Ω. Adding the series resistor gives 50 + 50 = 100 Ω. Combination networks are worked from the inside out, in the same way arithmetic follows an order of operations.

questions.subTitle: Resistors & Capacitors
questions.text: A low-pass RC filter is added to a mechanical switch to remove contact bounce. In this filter the capacitor is placed:

options.A: In series with the signal path
options.B: In series with both the resistor and the output
options.C: Between the logic gate output and the supply rail
options.D: In parallel with the output, with the resistor in series

questions.commentary: With the resistor in the signal path and the capacitor across the output, the capacitor charges through the resistor and smooths the rapid make and break of the contacts into one clean transition. Reversing the two components, with the capacitor in series, gives a high-pass filter instead, which blocks DC and passes fast signals.

questions.subTitle: Flow Diagrams
questions.text: In a flow diagram, which symbol represents a yes or no branch such as "temperature above 30 °C?"

options.A: Diamond
options.B: Rounded rectangle
options.C: Parallelogram
options.D: Rectangle

questions.commentary: A diamond marks a decision, with two paths leaving it. A rounded rectangle is a terminator marking start or end, a parallelogram is input or output such as reading a sensor or writing to a display, and a plain rectangle is a process. Flowcharts separate what the system must do from how it will be coded.

questions.subTitle: Sensor Inputs
questions.text: A reversing aid must measure how far a vehicle is from the nearest obstacle. The most appropriate sensor is:

options.A: Hygrometer
options.B: Photoresistor
options.C: Ultrasonic
options.D: Accelerometer

questions.commentary: An ultrasonic sensor emits a pulse and times the returning echo, giving a digital distance reading that suits parking sensors and robotics. A hygrometer reads humidity and air temperature, a photoresistor light level, and an accelerometer motion, vibration or tilt. Matching the sensor to the physical quantity is the first step in specifying the input stage.

questions.subTitle: Logic
questions.text: An alarm must sound only when the door sensor and the motion sensor are both active. Which gate is required, and what is its output when only one input is 1?

options.A: OR, output 1
options.B: AND, output 0
options.C: OR, output 0
options.D: NOT, output 0

questions.commentary: AND outputs 1 only when every input is 1, so a single active sensor leaves the output at 0. A truth table for two inputs has 2² = 4 rows, and only the final row of an AND table gives an output of 1. OR would trigger on either sensor alone, which is not what the specification asks for.

questions.subTitle: Output Devices
questions.text: A microcontroller pin can only be fully on or fully off, yet it is used to vary the speed of a DC motor. This is achieved by:

options.A: Pulse width modulation, varying the proportion of time the pin is on
options.B: Changing the supply voltage at the pin
options.C: Adding a resistor in series with the pin
options.D: Switching the pin into analogue input mode

questions.commentary: Switching rapidly and varying the duty cycle makes a device that responds to average power behave as though it were receiving an intermediate voltage. The same technique dims an LED, because the eye averages the flicker. A servo is the exception: it reads the width of each individual pulse to set its angle rather than responding to average power.

questions.subTitle: Communication Protocols
questions.text: A battery-powered fitness band must sync with a phone about a metre away and run for days on one charge. The most appropriate protocol is:

options.A: 5G, for its ultra-low latency
options.B: Wi-Fi, for its higher data rate
options.C: Any of the three, since power consumption is comparable
options.D: Bluetooth, for its very low power consumption over short range

questions.commentary: Bluetooth is built for low-power peer-to-peer links of around ten metres and needs no router or network subscription, which is why wearables, earbuds and medical sensors use it. Wi-Fi offers more speed at higher power and requires an access point, while 5G reaches kilometres and suits vehicles and large-scale IoT rather than a device living on a coin cell.

questions.subTitle: Production system types
questions.text: Before the Industrial Revolution, manufacturing was characterised by:

options.A: Assembly lines using standardised parts
options.B: Craft production by skilled artisans working from start to finish
options.C: Computer-integrated manufacturing
options.D: Mass production of identical goods

questions.commentary: A single artisan, often after an apprenticeship of up to seven years, made each item complete. Output was low, cost per unit high and no two pieces identical. The moving assembly line was the turning point away from this, trading variety for volume and consistency.

questions.subTitle: Production system types
questions.text: A luxury car manufacturer robot-welds the body shell but hand-stitches the interior trim. This is best described as:

options.A: Craft production
options.B: Continuous production
options.C: Mechanised production
options.D: Hybrid production

questions.commentary: Hybrid production deliberately combines systems, using automation where repeatability and speed matter and skilled hand work where the customer is paying for craft. It balances customisation against efficiency, at the cost of being more complex to manage and needing both skilled workers and machinery.

questions.subTitle: Advantages & disadvantages
questions.text: Which is a genuine disadvantage of assembly line production?

options.A: It is inflexible, and one breakdown can stop the entire line
options.B: It cannot achieve economies of scale
options.C: It requires highly skilled workers at every station
options.D: Quality varies noticeably between batches

questions.commentary: The line is optimised around one product, so design changes are slow and costly, and because stations run in series a stoppage anywhere halts everything downstream. Its strengths are the opposite of the distractors: strong economies of scale, consistent output and a reduced need for skilled labour, though the repetitive work carries its own cost in worker dissatisfaction.

questions.subTitle: Advantages & disadvantages
questions.text: The distinguishing feature of computer-integrated manufacturing (CIM) is that it:

options.A: Removes the need for any quality control
options.B: Relies on manual assembly of every component
options.C: Integrates design, production, quality control and logistics into one data system
options.D: Supports only craft-based customisation

questions.commentary: Because the whole enterprise shares one data model, a change in CAD can flow straight into manufacturing instructions, variants can be produced without retooling, and distributors can see production data globally. The costs are a very high setup investment, staff restructuring, and the risk that a software fault stops everything at once.

questions.subTitle: Scale of production
questions.text: Steel mills, petroleum refineries and paper mills run without stopping. This scale of production is:

options.A: Continuous production
options.B: Batch production
options.C: One-off production
options.D: Mass customisation

questions.commentary: Continuous, or process, production runs around the clock on fully automated plant, because stopping and restarting the process is either impossible or extremely expensive. Batch production makes tens to thousands of units at a time, such as a seasonal clothing range, and one-off production makes a single unit.

questions.subTitle: Scale of production
questions.text: Build-to-order laptops and made-to-measure dental aligners are examples of:

options.A: One-off production
options.B: Batch production
options.C: Continuous production
options.D: Mass customisation

questions.commentary: Mass customisation uses CIM and flexible automation to produce individually configured units at close to mass-production efficiency. It is worth asking how much real design freedom the customer has: the configuration is usually a wide but fixed menu of options the system can build without retooling.

questions.subTitle: Factors influencing choice
questions.text: A team needs one polymer bracket for testing next week, and later expects to produce a million of them. The appropriate techniques are:

options.A: Injection moulding for both
options.B: 3D printing for both
options.C: 3D printing for the single part, injection moulding for the production run
options.D: Sand casting for the single part, 3D printing for the production run

questions.commentary: Scale is the factor that decides here. A single part cannot justify tooling that costs tens or hundreds of thousands, so a flexible tool-free process wins. At a million units the tooling is spread across every part made and the per-unit cost falls far below any additive process. Material, geometry, available equipment and environmental impact then refine the choice.

questions.subTitle: Reverse engineering
questions.text: In a reverse engineering teardown, redundancy assessment means:

options.A: Fitting backup power supplies before disassembly begins
options.B: Identifying parts that are unnecessary or overdesigned and could be simplified or removed
options.C: Filming the disassembly from several angles
options.D: Making duplicate parts so the original can be kept intact

questions.commentary: It is the last of the six steps, after visual examination, disassembly, component analysis, manufacturing analysis and assembly analysis. Removing or combining parts that do no essential work cuts cost, material and assembly time, which is exactly the reasoning design for manufacture builds on.

questions.subTitle: Production & design aesthetics
questions.text: A stamped car body panel is stiffer and more impact resistant than the flat sheet it was pressed from. This is because stamping:

options.A: Anneals the metal, relaxing its internal stresses
options.B: Adds a hardened surface coating
options.C: Increases the thickness of the sheet
options.D: Work hardens the metal by tangling dislocations in its crystal structure

questions.commentary: Deforming metal cold creates and tangles dislocations, so it resists further deformation: harder and stronger, but less ductile. Cold rolling produces the same effect along with a flat reflective finish, and a paperclip bent repeatedly eventually snaps for the same reason. Annealing reverses it by letting the dislocations relax.

questions.subTitle: Production & design aesthetics
questions.text: Compared with a hand-carved chair, a CNC machined chair typically shows:

options.A: Precise repeatable joints, clean lines and identical reproductions
options.B: Greater variation between individual pieces
options.C: Less precise joints and lower structural rigidity
options.D: Visible layer lines across every surface

questions.commentary: Machining produces consistent mortise-and-tenon joints and identical copies, which improves rigidity and gives a clean, uniform look. Hand carving offers visible craftsmanship and a unique piece each time, with more variation in joint quality. Layer lines belong to fused deposition printing, not machining.

questions.subTitle: Designer's Responsibilities
questions.text: A team is asked to justify a design decision in terms of sustainable development. Which test does that require them to apply?

options.A: The product meets the safety standard that applies to its category
options.B: The product generates repeat sales over a predictable replacement cycle
options.C: The product is made under a certified quality management system
options.D: The product meets present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own

questions.commentary: This is the reference definition of sustainable development, set out by the UN World Commission on Environment and Development in 1987. It puts people who do not yet exist into the design equation, which is what separates it from safety, quality or commercial tests. Those matter, but none of them asks what the decision costs anyone beyond the current user.

questions.subTitle: Designer's Responsibilities
questions.text: The triple bottom line evaluates a design decision against which three accounts?

options.A: Cost, time and quality
options.B: People, planet and profit
options.C: Form, function and finish
options.D: Reduce, reuse and recycle

questions.commentary: People covers users, workers and communities, planet the environmental impact across the whole life cycle, and profit the economic viability of the work. Good design tries to satisfy all three; poor design sacrifices two to maximise the third, which is exactly what happened at Minamata.

questions.subTitle: Designer's Responsibilities
questions.text: Microplastics are best described as:

options.A: Plastic fragments under 5 mm, formed as plastic breaks apart without ever decomposing
options.B: A biodegradable substitute for polyethylene packaging
options.C: Additives mixed into textiles to increase their strength
options.D: Particles that dissolve harmlessly once they reach water

questions.commentary: Plastic fragments under UV, abrasion and washing rather than biodegrading, so the pieces simply get smaller and persist. Synthetic clothing fibres, tyre wear and single-use packaging are the main sources, and the particles have now been found in drinking water and human tissue. Like PFAS, this is a harm a designer specifies into a product invisibly at the point of sale.

questions.subTitle: Safety & Standardisation
questions.text: For a designer, the main value of a standard such as ISO 8124 or ASTM F963 is that it:

options.A: Guarantees the product will sell well
options.B: Removes the need to prototype and test
options.C: States exactly which requirements the product must meet, reducing guesswork and legal risk
options.D: Allows any material to be used without restriction

questions.commentary: Toy safety standards specify material toxicology, flammability, small-parts hazards, sharp edges and mechanical abuse testing, so the designer knows what has to be satisfied rather than guessing. Standards are mostly written after somebody has already been hurt, which is why compliance is documented rather than assumed.

questions.subTitle: Safety & Standardisation
questions.text: A CE, FCC or CCC mark on a product tells a consumer that:

options.A: It has been independently tested against a recognised standard
options.B: The product was manufactured in that region
options.C: The product is fully recyclable
options.D: The manufacturer holds a patent on the design

questions.commentary: Certification marks let a buyer trust a product they cannot test themselves. They carry weight because enforcement agencies such as the CPSC in the United States and the ACCC in Australia can order recalls, fines and import bans, and because retailers who face liability will not stock uncertified goods.

questions.subTitle: Safety & Standardisation
questions.text: A replacement bolt bought in one country threads correctly into a nut manufactured in another. Which principle makes this possible?

options.A: Every part is made unique so that it can be traced back to its maker
options.B: Products are designed so that only the original manufacturer can repair them
options.C: Safety testing is carried out after production rather than during design
options.D: Parts made to a shared specification are identical within a tolerance, so they can be swapped without hand fitting

questions.commentary: Before interchangeability, components were hand fitted to one another, so a broken part meant returning the product to a maker who could file a new one to suit. A shared specification with a stated tolerance means any conforming part fits any conforming assembly. That is what makes spare parts, servicing, recalls and global supply chains workable, so standardisation serves manufacturers as directly as it serves user safety.

questions.subTitle: Planned Obsolescence
questions.text: In the 1920s the Phoebus cartel agreed to limit lightbulb life to around 1,000 hours, even though longer-lasting bulbs were technically possible. This is an example of:

options.A: Style obsolescence
options.B: Functional obsolescence
options.C: Technological obsolescence
options.D: Social obsolescence

questions.commentary: Functional obsolescence means the product is engineered to wear out or fail sooner than it needs to. The cartel is the clearest documented case, and the same manufacturer's flashlight bulbs of the 1930s were redesigned to burn brighter and die faster. Style and social obsolescence work on perception instead, and technological obsolescence on compatibility.

questions.subTitle: Planned Obsolescence
questions.text: A smartphone that still works but can no longer receive operating system updates, leaving it insecure and incompatible with current apps, illustrates:

options.A: Style obsolescence
options.B: Social obsolescence
options.C: Technological obsolescence
options.D: The circular economy

questions.commentary: The hardware has not failed; withdrawn software support has made continued use impractical. This is the form of obsolescence most often accused of being deliberate, and the hardest to separate from honest engineering, since ageing batteries and rising security requirements are also real constraints.

questions.subTitle: Planned Obsolescence
questions.text: A pair of intact bell-bottom jeans from 1975 that nobody will wear today has been affected by:

options.A: Functional obsolescence
options.B: Technological obsolescence
options.C: Kaizen
options.D: Style obsolescence

questions.commentary: Nothing has broken and no technology has moved on: only fashion has shifted, which is what makes the item unwearable. Style obsolescence drives the fastest replacement cycles of all, and fast fashion is the industrial-scale version, contributing 8 to 10% of global CO₂ emissions with 87% of textile waste going to landfill.

questions.subTitle: Planned Obsolescence
questions.text: A handbag maker raises its prices and demand rises rather than falls. Which explanation fits, and how does it connect to obsolescence?

options.A: The price itself signals prestige, so the product is bought as a status marker, which sustains style obsolescence
options.B: Buyers always take the cheapest option available, so the increase must have been matched by competitors
options.C: Buyers are prioritising repairability and long service life
options.D: Buyers are responding to environmental certification rather than price

questions.commentary: For goods of this kind, demand increases with price because the price is part of what is being bought. The effect is named after Thorstein Veblen. It matters in an obsolescence discussion because status value decays as soon as the signal is widely shared, which is what drives the seasonal replacement cycles of style obsolescence and the waste those cycles produce.

questions.subTitle: Universal Design
questions.text: Which statement best captures what universal design asks of a product?

options.A: It is supplied as a standard version plus a separate adapted version for users with impairments
options.B: It is sized as accurately as possible to the 50th percentile user
options.C: It is usable by as many people as possible in its standard form, without adaptation or a specialised version
options.D: It complies with accessibility legislation in at least one market

questions.commentary: Universal design targets the widest possible audience in a single mainstream product, regardless of age or ability. The standard definition is design usable by all people to the greatest extent possible without needing adaptation. A separate adapted version fails that test twice over, since it stigmatises the people who need it and adds the cost of a second product line.

questions.subTitle: Universal Design
questions.text: Which principle of universal design requires that necessary information reaches the user regardless of ambient conditions or their sensory abilities?

options.A: Perceptible information
options.B: Equitable use
options.C: Low physical effort
options.D: Flexibility in use

questions.commentary: Perceptible information is the principle behind repeating a message across more than one sensory channel, such as pairing a warning colour with a symbol or a sound with a vibration. Equitable use concerns whether the design serves diverse abilities without singling anyone out, and low physical effort concerns fatigue during use.

questions.subTitle: Universal Design
questions.text: Inclusive design aims at mainstream products rather than a separate range of "special needs" versions mainly because separate versions:

options.A: Are technically impossible to manufacture
options.B: Cannot be certified to any safety standard
options.C: Are prohibited by disability legislation
options.D: Stigmatise the people who use them and add cost

questions.commentary: A parallel product line marks its users out as different and is usually more expensive, because it is made in far smaller volumes. The goal is one product that works for everyone, which is why inclusive design extends user-centred design by deliberately including people who are otherwise overlooked: older users, pregnant women, disabled people and the temporarily injured.

questions.subTitle: Universal Design
questions.text: Accessibility legislation exists in many countries and shapes what a designer must consider. What does such legislation typically require?

options.A: That a separately adapted version of each product is placed on the market
options.B: That reasonable provision is made for people with disabilities in access, employment and the use of products and services
options.C: That accessibility is assessed only after a product has reached the market
options.D: That every product is made usable by 100% of the population

questions.commentary: The Americans with Disabilities Act 1990, the Disability Discrimination Act 1992 in Australia and the Equality Act 2010 in the UK differ in detail, but all turn on reasonable provision rather than a guarantee of universal usability. For a designer this sets a floor, not a target: meeting the legal minimum is not the same as designing inclusively, and the wider percentile question still has to be answered.

questions.subTitle: Designing for Percentiles
questions.text: Why is there no meaningfully "average" person to design for?

options.A: Body dimensions are not correlated, so short arms do not imply short legs
options.B: Averages cannot be calculated accurately from anthropometric data
options.C: Only children need inclusive design consideration
options.D: Percentile data applies only to standing height

questions.commentary: Someone can be 5th percentile in arm reach and 95th percentile in torso height at the same time. The Union soldiers census of 1850 makes the point: the average height was five feet eight inches, but no individual soldier was average across every relevant dimension at once. A product built to the 50th percentile in every dimension therefore fits almost nobody precisely.

questions.subTitle: Designing for Percentiles
questions.text: Which percentile range do designers normally target?

options.A: 1st to 99th
options.B: 25th to 75th
options.C: The 50th percentile alone
options.D: 5th to 95th

questions.commentary: This range covers the central 90% of the population, so the product must work for the smallest plausible user in the critical dimension and for the largest. A seat, for example, needs adjustment to serve both ends of that band rather than a single fixed setting.

questions.subTitle: Designing for Percentiles
questions.text: Which statement about the limits of inclusive design is most accurate?

options.A: Any product can be made universally usable if enough effort is invested
options.B: Inclusive design applies only to public buildings and transport
options.C: Users beyond the chosen percentile range will still need adapted solutions, and designers should be able to justify where the boundary sits
options.D: Percentile data removes the need to test with real users

questions.commentary: Naming the limit is a more sophisticated answer than claiming everything can be made universal. Excluding the outermost 5% at each end is a deliberate compromise, not an oversight, and stating where the line is drawn and why is what an examiner is looking for.

questions.subTitle: Design for Extremes
questions.text: Text-to-speech and voice control were developed for users who could not read a screen, and are now used by millions of people while driving or cooking. This illustrates:

options.A: Planned obsolescence driving repeat purchases
options.B: The curb-cut effect, where solving for the extreme improves the product for everyone
options.C: Designing for the 50th percentile user
options.D: Safety standardisation enforced by regulators

questions.commentary: The constraint could not be met by enlarging or brightening text, so it forced a different interaction model entirely. That is the structural reason the strategy works: a hard constraint prevents incremental tinkering with the status quo. Kerb ramps, built for wheelchair users and now used with prams, suitcases and trolleys, gave the effect its name.

questions.subTitle: Design for Extremes
questions.text: A vegetable peeler is developed around the constraint that its users have arthritis. Which set of features does that constraint demand, and what is the wider effect?

options.A: A left-handed blade orientation, which suits only part of the population
options.B: A faster cutting action for professional kitchens, which suits high-volume users
options.C: A blade guard sized for young children, which limits the tool to family use
options.D: Low grip force, a large non-slip handle and pressure kept off the finger joints, which reduces hand fatigue for every user

questions.commentary: Arthritis rules out the thin smooth metal handle entirely and forces an oversized soft handle worked with a palm grip rather than a pinch. The resulting tool is easier for everyone, which is the design for extremes argument: a constraint that looks narrow produces a solution the general population prefers. OXO Good Grips is the standard example, and it reshaped the whole kitchen tools market.

questions.subTitle: Design for Extremes
questions.text: A writing machine is built for a single blind user so that they can produce letters legible to sighted readers, with no market in mind. Its mechanism later becomes standard office equipment. This sequence supports the argument that:

options.A: Designing for an extreme constraint can produce a solution the general population adopts
options.B: Development should begin only once a market has been identified
options.C: Accessibility features add cost without producing wider benefit
options.D: A design for extremes strategy applies only to medical equipment

questions.commentary: The constraint was absolute: the user could not check the page, so the mechanism had to place characters reliably without sight. Solving that produced the typewriter, and carbon paper arrived as a by-product of needing to transfer ink consistently. Designing at the edge of the population removes the compromises that a comfortable average user would have tolerated, and the result is usually better for everyone.

questions.subTitle: Four Pleasures Framework
questions.text: What does the four-pleasure framework give a designer that a usability checklist does not?

options.A: Language for the physical, social, psychological and ideological responses a product provokes, so those reactions can be designed for and argued about
options.B: A method for calculating the manufacturing cost of a design decision
options.C: A ranking of materials by their durability in service
options.D: A percentile range for sizing a product to its user population

questions.commentary: Usability establishes whether a product can be operated. The four pleasures, proposed by the anthropologist Lionel Tiger and later applied to products, cover why a user wants to keep using it: physio-pleasure from the senses and the body, socio-pleasure from what it signals to others, psycho-pleasure from feeling competent, and ideo-pleasure from matching a user's values. Naming them turns a reaction that would be dismissed as personal taste into a design decision that can be defended.

questions.subTitle: Four Pleasures Framework
questions.text: The ribbed grip of a cold glass bottle, secure and satisfying in the hand, delivers:

options.A: Socio-pleasure
options.B: Psycho-pleasure
options.C: Ideo-pleasure
options.D: Physio-pleasure

questions.commentary: Physio-pleasure arrives through the body and the senses: touch, grip, temperature, weight, sound and smell. Nothing social or intellectual is involved in the feel of the bottle itself, which is why this maps onto Norman's visceral level.

questions.subTitle: Four Pleasures Framework
questions.text: A buyer chooses a particular watch because of what owning it signals to colleagues. This is:

options.A: Physio-pleasure
options.B: Psycho-pleasure
options.C: Socio-pleasure
options.D: Ideo-pleasure

questions.commentary: Socio-pleasure comes from relationships, belonging and the standing a product confers. The purchase is being made for what the object says to other people rather than for how it feels in the hand or how well it keeps time.

questions.subTitle: Four Pleasures Framework
questions.text: An interface that responds predictably to every input, so a new user feels in control and competent within minutes, is delivering:

options.A: Physio-pleasure
options.B: Psycho-pleasure
options.C: Socio-pleasure
options.D: Ideo-pleasure

questions.commentary: Psycho-pleasure is cognitive and emotional: the satisfaction of understanding a product and mastering it. It corresponds to Norman's behavioural level, and it is the layer most closely tied to conventional usability, which is exactly why usability alone is a floor rather than a goal.

questions.subTitle: Four Pleasures Framework
questions.text: Choosing a product made from recycled ocean plastic because it matches the buyer's environmental beliefs is an example of:

options.A: Physio-pleasure
options.B: Psycho-pleasure
options.C: Socio-pleasure
options.D: Ideo-pleasure

questions.commentary: Ideo-pleasure comes from a product agreeing with the user's values and beliefs, independent of how it looks or performs. Material choice is one of the most direct ways to trigger it, which is why sustainability claims sit alongside aesthetics in a material justification.

questions.subTitle: The ACT Model
questions.text: Which of Donald Norman's three levels covers the immediate sensory reaction to how something looks, feels and sounds?

options.A: Visceral
options.B: Reflective
options.C: Behavioural
options.D: Functional

questions.commentary: The visceral level is the pre-conscious first reaction, and it aligns with physio-pleasure and with the Attract stage of the ACT model. Behavioural covers use and performance, and reflective covers meaning, values and identity.

questions.subTitle: The ACT Model
questions.text: The Converse stage of the ACT model aligns with which level and pleasure?

options.A: Visceral level and physio-pleasure
options.B: Behavioural level and psycho-pleasure
options.C: Reflective level and ideo-pleasure
options.D: Reflective level and socio-pleasure

questions.commentary: Converse is the stage of actually using the product, so it depends on clear affordances, consistent feedback and familiar population stereotypes such as turning a knob clockwise for on. If the product cannot hold a predictable conversation with the user, no amount of attraction will keep them.

questions.subTitle: The ACT Model
questions.text: The Transact stage of the ACT model refers to:

options.A: The moment of purchase and payment
options.B: The first visual impression of the product
options.C: The deeper meaning and attachment that produce continued use and loyalty
options.D: The manufacturing and assembly stage

questions.commentary: Transact is the long-term relationship, built through personalisation, community features and values-aligned details such as a carbon savings display. Despite its name it is not the sale: it is the reflective level, where socio-pleasure and ideo-pleasure turn a customer into an advocate.

questions.subTitle: The ACT Model
questions.text: The Juicy Salif lemon squeezer is difficult to use yet remains a design classic. In framework terms it:

options.A: Succeeds at every level, which is why it sells
options.B: Succeeds behaviourally but fails viscerally
options.C: Demonstrates that usability is the only thing that matters
options.D: Fails at the behavioural level but succeeds strongly at the reflective one

questions.commentary: As a juicer it performs poorly, so psycho-pleasure is weak. What it delivers is socio-pleasure, in the conversations and sophistication it signals, and ideo-pleasure for buyers who share its design philosophy. Without the framework a designer would score it a failure, when it is actually meeting a different and equally real need. It is an exception rather than a model for a phone or a medical device.

questions.subTitle: The ACT Model
questions.text: A retailer offers free one-to-one technical help that has nothing to do with that day's purchase. Which ACT stage does this serve?

options.A: Transact
options.B: Attract
options.C: Converse
options.D: None, because no product is sold

questions.commentary: Support given independently of a sale builds the ongoing relationship that turns a customer into an advocate, which is the reflective payoff of the Transact stage. In the same space, an uncluttered glass storefront does the attracting, and staff carrying the point-of-sale system so that no queue ever forms keeps the conversation moving.

questions.subTitle: Sustainability Strategies
questions.text: Which of these is a bottom-up sustainability strategy?

options.A: An international treaty setting carbon reduction targets
options.B: A United Nations commission report defining sustainable development
options.C: A national government recycling mandate
options.D: A community group planting native grasses to stabilise coastal dunes

questions.commentary: Bottom-up strategies begin with individuals and local communities acting on the principle of thinking globally and acting locally. Treaties, commission reports and national mandates all impose change downwards from institutions, and their common criticism is that they set goals without clear methods or clear responsibility for delivery.

questions.subTitle: Sustainability Strategies
questions.text: Designing a product so that it can be taken apart at end of life primarily addresses which sustainability decision area?

options.A: Waste, because materials can be separated and recovered
options.B: Energy consumption during use
options.C: Pollution from manufacturing solvents
options.D: Social equity in the supply chain

questions.commentary: Design for disassembly is the practical route to minimising waste, since mixed and bonded materials cannot be economically separated. The other decision areas designers weigh are pollution from hazardous processes and finishes, energy in manufacture and use, longevity through repair and upgrade, and the choice of low-impact or renewable materials.

questions.subTitle: Datschefski's Five Principles
questions.text: Greenwashing is best described as:

options.A: Manufacturing products from recycled green glass
options.B: Marketing a product as sustainable on the strength of one small or superficial environmental feature
options.C: Composting biodegradable production waste
options.D: Using green packaging to indicate recyclability

questions.commentary: A product with 5% recycled content advertised as eco-friendly while the rest is virgin material is the standard case. Datschefski developed his five principles precisely because words like green and natural carry no measurable standard, so a claim could not be checked against anything.

questions.subTitle: Datschefski's Five Principles
questions.text: A backpack made from recycled PET bottles, designed so it can be recycled again at end of life, satisfies which principle?

options.A: Solar
options.B: Safe
options.C: Cyclic
options.D: Social

questions.commentary: Cyclic requires that materials return to a loop after use, either by breaking down naturally or by being reprocessed into the material stream, so a product that ends in landfill fails it. Solar concerns the energy used to make and run the product, safe concerns toxicity at every stage, and social concerns the conditions under which it was made.

questions.subTitle: Datschefski's Five Principles
questions.text: A smartphone that replaces a separate camera, music player and navigation device is most often cited as an example of which principle?

options.A: Cyclic
options.B: Safe
options.C: Social
options.D: Efficient

questions.commentary: Efficient calls for a design to use around one tenth of the materials and energy of what it replaces, and combining functions is the usual route, since one device doing four jobs displaces the material cost of three others. It is worth noting that a product can score well on one principle while failing others badly.

questions.subTitle: Datschefski's Five Principles
questions.text: Which principle is breached when a supplier pays below a living wage or sources minerals from a conflict zone?

options.A: Social
options.B: Cyclic
options.C: Solar
options.D: Efficient

questions.commentary: Social covers safe working conditions, fair trade, workers' rights and benefit to the communities involved, including conflict-free sourcing. Its presence in the list is what stops sustainability being treated as a purely environmental question.

questions.subTitle: Triple Bottom Line
questions.text: The triple bottom line measures the success of a product or organisation across:

options.A: Cost, quality and delivery time
options.B: Reduce, reuse and recycle
options.C: People, planet and profit
options.D: Materials, energy and waste

questions.commentary: People covers social equity, fair labour and community wellbeing, planet covers environmental health and resource use, and profit covers economic viability. Reporting all three together is the point: an organisation cannot claim success on one while quietly failing the others. The framework is credited to John Elkington.

questions.subTitle: Triple Bottom Line
questions.text: A profitable product with a genuinely low environmental impact is manufactured using exploited labour. In triple bottom line terms it:

options.A: Satisfies people and planet but fails profit
options.B: Satisfies profit and planet but fails people
options.C: Satisfies people and profit but fails planet
options.D: Satisfies all three dimensions

questions.commentary: Genuine sustainability sits where all three circles overlap, so satisfying two is not enough. The equivalent failures are a profitable, fairly made product that pollutes heavily, and an environmentally and socially sound product that cannot be sold at a viable price.

questions.subTitle: Balancing the Three Ps
questions.text: A client resists switching to renewable energy in manufacturing because of the upfront cost. Which strategy from this topic addresses that objection most directly?

options.A: Phased implementation, spreading the transition cost over a longer timeframe
options.B: Dropping the planet dimension from the analysis
options.C: Raising the retail price immediately to cover it
options.D: Treating profit as irrelevant to sustainability

questions.commentary: Phasing spreads the investment so short-term profit is not hit all at once, and it pairs with stakeholder education about reduced material costs, lower regulatory risk and stronger brand loyalty. Life-cycle thinking makes the same case numerically, since costs that look high at the design stage are often recovered across the product's life.

questions.subTitle: Balancing the Three Ps
questions.text: In a triple bottom line analysis, which of the following counts as a diffuse stakeholder?

options.A: The client who commissioned the design
options.B: The end user who buys the product
options.C: The manufacturer producing the product
options.D: Future generations and ecosystems far from where the product is made

questions.commentary: Client, user and manufacturer are direct stakeholders; factory workers, neighbouring communities and competitors are indirect; future generations and distant ecosystems are diffuse. Counting the full set is what makes a hidden cost visible: a decision that looks purely financial when only the client is considered stops looking that way once everyone affected is on the list.

questions.subTitle: Linear vs Circular Economy
questions.text: Which phrase describes the traditional linear economic model?

options.A: Reuse, recycle, recover
options.B: Take, make, consume, dispose
options.C: Reduce, repair, refurbish
options.D: Design, manufacture, recycle

questions.commentary: The linear model runs in one direction and ends in landfill or incineration, treating resources as unlimited and disposal as inevitable. It also depends on non-renewable energy and virgin material inputs. A circular system replaces that final step so materials re-enter production instead of leaving the system.

questions.subTitle: Linear vs Circular Economy
questions.text: In a circular economy, the concept of end-of-life is replaced by:

options.A: Taking, making and disposing at lower cost
options.B: More efficient use of landfill capacity
options.C: Shorter planned obsolescence cycles
options.D: Reducing, reusing, recycling and recovering materials

questions.commentary: The principle applies across production, distribution and consumption, so no stage of the system is designated as finished. PET bottles collected and remanufactured into new bottles or textiles, and paper recycled repeatedly into new paper, are the everyday illustrations. It is worth asking how closed a loop really is, since most plastics are downcycled once or twice at best.

questions.subTitle: Design-for Strategies
questions.text: Which of the following is an example of dematerialisation?

options.A: Email replacing posted letters and faxes
options.B: Making a product heavier so that it lasts longer
options.C: Adding protective packaging to reduce transport damage
options.D: Specifying a non-recyclable material for extra strength

questions.commentary: Dematerialisation is a steady fall in the material or energy needed to deliver the same service. Miniaturised electronics and streaming replacing physical discs are the other standard cases. The impact does not disappear, since servers and networks have footprints of their own, but the resource input per unit of value delivered drops sharply.

questions.subTitle: Design-for Strategies
questions.text: Jevons observed in 1865 that more efficient steam engines led to greater total coal consumption, not less. The lesson for designers is that:

options.A: Efficiency improvements are technically impossible to achieve
options.B: Coal is a renewable resource when used efficiently
options.C: Efficiency gains can be cancelled out by increased demand, so they cannot be assumed to cut total consumption
options.D: Older technologies always consume fewer resources overall

questions.commentary: Cheaper, better steam power spread into more factories, trains and ships, so total coal use rose even as each engine used less. The modern equivalent is a more economical car that makes driving cheap enough to do more of. Countering the rebound effect needs systemic and behavioural design alongside efficiency, such as prompts that encourage running an appliance only when full.

questions.subTitle: Design-for Strategies
questions.text: A laptop is designed with modular components so a user can replace a failed part rather than the whole machine. This is:

options.A: Dematerialisation
options.B: Design for process
options.C: Extended producer responsibility
options.D: Design for longevity

questions.commentary: Longevity is pursued through repairability, upgradability, durable materials, aesthetics that do not date, and an emotional attachment that makes users reluctant to discard something still working. Keeping a product in use is the cheapest loop in the circular model, since a device lasting ten years rather than two removes four replacements from the waste stream.

questions.subTitle: Biodegradable Materials
questions.text: Why are biodegradable materials preferred within a circular economy model?

options.A: They break down into water, minerals and organic matter, returning nutrients to the soil
options.B: They are always cheaper to produce than conventional plastics
options.C: They persist in landfill without generating methane
options.D: They require more energy to manufacture, which offsets their impact

questions.commentary: Completing the biological cycle keeps material out of landfill, avoids the methane produced by anaerobic decomposition of buried organic waste, and returns organic matter to the soil. Conventional plastics do the opposite, fragmenting into microplastics that enter food chains and waterways rather than decomposing.

questions.subTitle: Biodegradable Materials
questions.text: What is the main limitation a designer must account for when specifying a biodegradable material?

options.A: They cannot be manufactured in large quantities
options.B: They are banned in most packaging regulations
options.C: Some require industrial composting conditions that may not exist where the product is thrown away
options.D: They degrade instantly on contact with air

questions.commentary: Specific temperature, humidity and microbial conditions are needed for many biodegradable polymers, and labelling alone achieves nothing if that infrastructure is absent at the point of disposal. The designer's responsibility is to specify an end-of-life pathway that is genuinely accessible to the user, not merely available in principle.

questions.subTitle: Recovery and Restoration
questions.text: The resin identification codes, the numbers 1 to 7 inside a triangle, exist mainly to:

options.A: Show the manufacturing date of the product
options.B: Let recyclers identify the polymer so it can be sorted into a compatible stream
options.C: Indicate the country of origin
options.D: Indicate the price grade of the plastic

questions.commentary: Code 1 is PET, 2 HDPE, 3 PVC, 4 LDPE, 5 PP, 6 PS and 7 other. Sorting matters because incompatible polymers contaminate a batch: a PET bottle carrying a PVC label is the standard example. Single-material components and clear marking avoid the cost of spectroscopic analysis at the recycling facility.

questions.subTitle: Recovery and Restoration
questions.text: Take-back legislation and extended producer responsibility schemes change a designer's incentives because:

options.A: The manufacturer pays for recovery, so a hard-to-disassemble design becomes a cost on its own balance sheet
options.B: They prohibit the use of plastics in consumer products
options.C: They set a maximum retail price for regulated products
options.D: They require every component to be biodegradable

questions.commentary: Once the cost of end-of-life handling returns to the producer rather than sitting in someone else's landfill bill, design for disassembly, single-material components and standardised fasteners all become financially rational. The WEEE Directive for electronics and packaging fee schemes scaled to recyclability both work this way.

questions.subTitle: Renewable Energy
questions.text: Why can a circular economy not genuinely run on fossil fuels?

options.A: Fossil fuels are more expensive than renewable sources everywhere
options.B: Renewable sources deliver more energy per unit of mass
options.C: Fossil-fuelled plants cannot supply factories continuously
options.D: Fossil fuels are consumed rather than recovered, and the resulting emissions are a waste stream the system cannot reabsorb

questions.commentary: Materials in a circular system can be recovered and restored, but burnt fuel cannot, and carbon dioxide accumulates in the atmosphere as effectively irreversible waste. Recycling, remanufacturing, composting and take-back logistics all need a continuous energy flow, so that flow has to come from sources that replenish rather than deplete.

questions.subTitle: Purpose of product analysis
questions.text: The primary purpose of product analysis and evaluation is to:

options.A: Reduce manufacturing cost
options.B: Increase the speed of production
options.C: Build a full understanding of what makes a product functional, appealing and competitive
options.D: Remove every weakness from the product

questions.commentary: Analysis asks what makes the product work, why people buy it and how it compares with rivals, and its output is actionable insight: a specific, implementable recommendation. Lower cost or faster production may follow, but they are consequences rather than the purpose.

questions.subTitle: Stakeholder involvement
questions.text: Which stakeholder gathers data from every other group and turns it into a single direction for further development?

options.A: Product designers
options.B: Engineers
options.C: Marketing staff
options.D: Product development managers

questions.commentary: Designers contribute on aesthetics, experience and sustainability, engineers on feasibility and manufacture, and marketing on trends, pricing and competition. The development manager acts as the bridge between those specialist views, which is what stops analysis becoming a set of disconnected opinions.

questions.subTitle: Stakeholder involvement
questions.text: Customer support staff are a valuable source of analysis data because they:

options.A: Hear the same real-world problems repeatedly, including failures that testing missed
options.B: Decide the aesthetics of the next version
options.C: Set the retail price of the product
options.D: Give final approval for market launch

questions.commentary: Support teams talk to users after purchase and at scale, which surfaces recurring pain points and the failures that only appear after extended use. Customer reviews serve the same function, and both reach problems that laboratory testing cannot reproduce.

questions.subTitle: SWOT analysis
questions.text: In a SWOT analysis, a market crowded with established and emerging competitor brands is classified as a:

options.A: Strength
options.B: Threat
options.C: Weakness
options.D: Opportunity

questions.commentary: Threats are negative and external, arising from the market, technology or regulation rather than from the product itself. The commonest error with this framework is placing an external factor in an internal quadrant: limited capacity in a design is a weakness, while rising demand for that product category is an opportunity.

questions.subTitle: SWOT analysis
questions.text: How does Porter's Five Forces differ from a SWOT analysis?

options.A: It analyses competitive intensity across a whole industry rather than a single product
options.B: It examines only the internal strengths of an organisation
options.C: It calculates the manufacturing cost of a product
options.D: It replaces SWOT entirely and is used instead of it

questions.commentary: The five forces are competitive rivalry, supplier power, buyer power, the threat of new entrants and the threat of substitution. SWOT examines one product against its own strengths and its market; Five Forces asks whether the industry it sits in is worth competing in at all, so the two are complementary.

questions.subTitle: Testing & reverse engineering
questions.text: A team records error rates and time on task while participants operate a new interface. This is:

options.A: Materials testing
options.B: Performance testing
options.C: Benchmarking
options.D: Usability testing

questions.commentary: Usability testing measures how easily the product can be operated, and its output is the identification of confusing interfaces and missing affordances. Performance testing checks the product against its functional specification for speed, load or accuracy, materials testing covers strength and durability, and benchmarking compares the result with competitors.

questions.subTitle: Testing & reverse engineering
questions.text: Designers carry out a teardown of a competitor's product mainly to:

options.A: Establish the correct retail price
options.B: Learn how it was made and assembled, and where its components fail
options.C: Produce marketing material
options.D: Dispose of the product safely

questions.commentary: Disassembly reveals component materials, manufacturing processes, the assembly sequence and the structural decisions behind them, which shows how a rival solved a problem and where cost or complexity has accumulated. Applied to a designer's own product, it exposes failure modes directly.

questions.subTitle: Benchmarking & opportunities
questions.text: Benchmarking shows a product leading its competitors, and no significant user complaints have been recorded. The appropriate decision is to:

options.A: Discontinue the product
options.B: Invest immediately in a full redesign
options.C: Leave the product unchanged
options.D: Reverse engineer a competitor and copy its approach

questions.commentary: Analysis leads to one of three decisions. Investment suits fixable weaknesses paired with a real market opportunity, discontinuation suits irreparable weaknesses in a declining market, and leaving a product unchanged is the right call when its strengths outweigh its weaknesses and its position is stable. Choosing on evidence rather than instinct is the point of the exercise.

questions.subTitle: Constructive discontent
questions.text: Which statement is an example of constructive discontent rather than simple criticism?

options.A: "This knife block is unhygienic and badly made."
options.B: "Nobody I know likes this knife block."
options.C: "The knife block should be discontinued immediately."
options.D: "Crumbs collect in the sealed slots of the knife block, which could be solved with removable, dishwasher-safe inserts."

questions.commentary: Constructive discontent names the specific failure and a route to fixing it, in the form of fails at X, which could be solved by Y. That turns a reaction into an actionable design brief, whereas criticism alone identifies a problem and stops, which demoralises a team without directing it.

questions.subTitle: Product analysis outcomes
questions.text: Why is product analysis described as an evidence base rather than an end in itself?

options.A: Because it grounds decisions in user reality and feeds a cycle of observing, analysing, deciding and iterating
options.B: Because it removes the need to build prototypes
options.C: Because it determines the retail price of the product
options.D: Because it guarantees the next version will succeed commercially

questions.commentary: Observation gathers test data, stakeholder views and teardowns; analysis applies SWOT, benchmarking and constructive discontent; the decision to improve, leave alone or discontinue follows from that evidence; and the cycle repeats. Along the way it prevents designing in isolation, reveals failure modes that only appear in real use, and builds stakeholder support for the changes that result.

questions.subTitle: LCA and environmental impacts
questions.text: Nitrogen and phosphorus runoff that causes algal blooms and oxygen depletion in waterways is assessed in an LCA under which impact category?

options.A: Eutrophication
options.B: Acidification
options.C: Ozone depletion
options.D: Resource depletion

questions.commentary: Eutrophication is the water pollution category, measured in kg phosphate equivalent. Acidification covers sulphur and nitrogen oxides forming acid rain, ozone depletion covers CFCs and HCFCs attacking stratospheric ozone, and resource depletion covers the extraction of finite fuels, minerals and rare earth elements.

questions.subTitle: LCA and environmental impacts
questions.text: Global warming potential is normally reported in which unit?

options.A: kg SO₂ equivalent
options.B: kg CO₂ equivalent
